acceptance_criteria.statement: A signed-in customer who submits a long URL receives a short link in the response.
Requesting a live short link redirects the requester to the long URL it was created from.
The click count reported for a link equals the number of clicks made on it, including repeated clicks from the same client, with no clicks missing.

A second and subsequent click on the same short link still reaches the service and is counted; the redirect response does not permit a browser or intermediary to go straight to the target without us seeing it.
A customer who asks for a specific short link gets that exact short link when it is available.
A request for a specific short link that is already taken is rejected rather than silently reassigned, and does not disclose the existing link's owner or target.
A customer can retrieve how their link has performed, and the click count returned reflects clicks already made.
After a customer deletes a link, clicking it no longer redirects to the original address.
After a link is deleted or reported as abusive, it stops working within the service's published time bound, measured from the delete or report.
A link is no longer redirected once it has expired, with default expiry about a month after creation.
The expiry of an individual link can be set or changed per link through configuration/data rather than requiring a code change.
A create, view-performance, or delete request without a valid signed-in session is refused.
A signed-in customer cannot view the performance of, delete, or otherwise interfere with a link belonging to another customer, and cannot tell from the response whether that link exists.
Clicking a short link succeeds with no credentials and no sign-in of any kind.
Requesting a short code that was never issued does not redirect and is not distinguishable from a code that exists but is not the requester's.

Given a set of issued short links, the short codes give no means of deriving or guessing other issued short codes; systematic guessing does not find links at a rate better than chance against the code space.
Stored customer credentials do not yield the original passwords to someone holding a full copy of the database.
A request carrying a customer's session is accepted by a service without that service making a call back to the login system on every request.

While one source is issuing requests at an abusive rate (link mining, existence scraping, or bulk junk-link creation), that source is throttled or refused and other customers' requests continue to be served.
Clicks continue to be redirected and counted while link creation or its dependencies are unavailable; when the system cannot do both, clicks are served in preference to accepting new links.
A long URL identified as phishing or malware is not turned into a working short link, and an existing link found to point at one stops redirecting.
Under a traffic spike in which a single short link takes a large fraction of total click traffic in a few minutes, clicks on that link continue to be served fast and counted.

constraints: PostgreSQL for data; no second database technology may be taken on
Redis is already run in-house and has capacity for this service
The deliverable is the HTTP API; there is no UI in this build
Build now for the two-year target scale rather than rewriting in eighteen months
Must not preclude later: customer-owned link domains, QR codes for a link, a paid permanent-link tier alongside expiring free links, and added database read capacity
Greenfield: the repository contains no existing application code to integrate with
output.goal: Signed-in customers can turn a long URL into a short link (generated or one they choose) that redirects whoever clicks it to the original address, while we count every one of those clicks for the life of the link and report the count back to the customer, delivered as an HTTP API.
in_scope: Customer sign-in before creating links, with passwords stored in a form that is still defensible if the database is stolen
A signed-in session that carries across our services without every request going back to a login system
Creating a short link from a long URL
Requesting a specific short link instead of the one we would generate, so links read as the customer's brand
Redirecting a click on a short link to the original address
Counting every click, on every click, for the life of the link, as a measured number rather than an estimate
Preventing a browser or intermediary from remembering where a short link went and skipping us on later clicks
Letting a customer see how a link has performed
Letting a customer delete a link they no longer want live
Reporting a link as abusive
Deleted and abuse-reported links ceasing to work quickly, against a stated number someone can hold us to
Link expiry about a month after creation, changeable per link rather than a number welded into the code
Per-customer ownership of links: a customer must not see or interfere with anybody else's links
Public, unauthenticated clicking (whoever clicks is not our customer and will never sign in)
Short links that cannot be found by guessing, and from which other existing links cannot be worked out
Continuing to serve real customers while under attack: link mining, existence scraping, junk-link storage burn, and attempts to knock the service over
Preventing use of the service as the front end of a phishing or malware campaign
A click path that stays fast and stays up even when the rest of the system is unhappy, preferring to serve a click over accepting a new link
Design headroom for 100 million link creations a day within two years without a rewrite
HTTP API as the deliverable, built on Java 21, Spring Boot, PostgreSQL and the existing Redis
non_functional: About 10 million link creations a day today, growing to 100 million a day within two years
Clicks run at about ten times the creation rate, and are much spikier than creations
A single link can carry a large fraction of a day's traffic within a few minutes
The great majority of clicks land on a small minority of links, and the same handful of links are hit repeatedly while hot
The click path must stay fast and stay available even when the rest of the system is degraded
Availability preference: serve a click correctly rather than accept a new link
Click counts must be exact for the life of the link, not sampled or estimated, and must not be lost to caching by browsers or intermediaries
Passwords stored so that theft of the database does not expose them
Sessions verifiable across services without a per-request call to the login system
Tenant isolation: no cross-customer visibility or interference
Short links are treated as secrets: unguessable and non-enumerable
Takedown latency for deleted or abuse-reported links must be a specific number the business can be held to, motivated by fraud takedown requests
Resilience to hostile traffic (mining, scraping, storage-burning junk links, denial of service) without degrading service to legitimate customers
The service must not become a usable front end for phishing or malware campaigns carrying our name
out_of_scope: Any user interface — the requirement states there is no UI in this build
Customer links on the customer's own domain (named as a future direction; must not be painted into a corner)
QR codes for a link (named as a future direction)
A paid tier of permanent, never-expiring links (named as a future direction; only expiry-per-link flexibility is asked for now)
Adding database read capacity / read replicas as click load grows (named as a future direction)
Customer account registration, sign-up or provisioning — the requirement says customers sign in but never says how accounts come to exist
Password reset, password change, multi-factor authentication, email verification and account recovery
Sign-out, session revocation and session lifetime rules — not mentioned
Roles, teams, or multiple users per customer — only 'per customer' ownership is stated
Editing a link after creation, including changing its target URL
Analytics beyond the click count (referrer, geography, device, unique visitors, time series) unless implied by 'see how a link has performed', which is not further specified
Billing, pricing, quotas and plan enforcement
An admin, moderation or support console for handling abuse reports
Who may report a link as abusive, and any review or appeal process around a takedown
Bulk link creation, import, export, or machine-to-machine API keys
Data retention, deletion of customer data, and privacy/regulatory obligations around click data
An interstitial or link-preview page before redirecting
Migration of any existing links or customers into this system
Deployment, infrastructure provisioning, CI/CD and on-call runbooks
Behaviour of clicks on a link after it expires beyond ceasing to redirect (e.g. renewal, grace periods)

answers.Q1: 60 seconds at the 99th percentile, measured from the API accepting the delete or the abuse report to the link ceasing to redirect. This is a published commitment the business will be held to, so the cache TTL is capped at 60s and active invalidation is required rather than optional. Design accordingly and state in the contract where the bound is enforced.
answers.Q2: Define a ThreatCheck port and ship two implementations in this build: a Postgres-backed domain/URL denylist checked synchronously on the create path, and a no-op. Do not integrate an external reputation service now -- the integration point must exist so one can be added without redesign. Independently of the checker, the floor is mandatory: scheme allowlist of http and https only, and rejection of private, loopback and link-local destinations, because the coming QR and preview features make this service fetch customer-supplied URLs and an SSRF proxy into our own network is the failure mode. Abuse takedown must be operable by a human under time pressure.

payload.note: Both answered. The takedown bound is a business commitment, not a design detail: publish it and hold the design to it. Threat checking follows the requirements brief -- build the integration point, plug nothing external in yet.

output.blast_radius: Nothing is in production and no caller exists, so the worst plausible outcome is not a customer-facing outage but a run that consumes its $120 ceiling and produces a service that cannot start. The concrete mechanism is the scaffold's Caffeine-only, Postgres-only shape colliding with a design that assumes Redis on the click path: the dependency lives in a protected pom.xml that only the design node may write, the connection settings live in a protected application.yml that only the implement node may write, and the local topology lives in a docker-compose.yml that no node may write at all. Get the ordering wrong and the failure surfaces late, at the verify barrier, as a context-load error inheriting from AbstractIntegrationTest - which fails every test class simultaneously and reads like a broken harness rather than a missing dependency. The second, quieter mechanism is the stale service/target/classes/db/migration/V1__create_links.sql from a previous run: gitignored, invisible in review, and applied by Flyway on any build that skips clean, producing a schema mismatch nobody can find in the diff. Detection is entirely through the mechanical gates - maven_compiles at design, tests_compile at test-contract, maven_verify and coverage_floor at verify - so the practical question for a reviewer is whether the design node froze a pom, an application.yml plan and a container harness that all three downstream nodes can actually build against, since none of them can renegotiate it afterwards.

breaking_changes.detail: Redis, a password KDF and a JWT library must be added, reversing the documented 'Caffeine only, no Redis' decision. pom.xml is a protected path and is in deny_paths for implement and author-tests, so the run stops at PENDING_APPROVAL the moment it is touched, and the two parallel branches cannot compile against anything the design node did not freeze there.
breaking_changes.mitigation: Design node adds the complete dependency set in a single write before the parallel fan-out (spring-boot-starter-data-redis, spring-security-crypto or argon2-jvm, a JWT library), so exactly one approval is spent and the frozen pom is what implement and author-tests both build against. Approver checks coordinates and scopes at the existing design human gate; no second window is needed.

breaking_changes.detail: UrlShortenerApplication is annotated @EnableCaching and CacheConfig currently supplies the one and only CacheManager. Introducing a Redis cache manager gives Spring two candidates and breaks context load for every test that extends AbstractIntegrationTest, including the scaffold's own theApplicationContextLoads.
breaking_changes.mitigation: Replace the body of CacheConfig rather than adding a parallel configuration class: keep the bean method name cacheManager and the LINKS_CACHE constant, or mark exactly one @Primary. Keep the Caffeine near-cache as an explicitly named second bean only if some component injects it by name.

breaking_changes.detail: The shipped default is expireAfterWrite=5m. Q1 commits the business to 60 seconds p99 from delete or report. A missed invalidation therefore leaves a deleted or abuse-blocked link redirecting for up to five minutes, breaching AC9 against a number quoted to fraud teams.
breaking_changes.mitigation: Lower the TTL in application.yml to at or below 60s in the same change that introduces active invalidation, so the TTL is a floor under the SLA rather than the mechanism; assert the bound in a test that deletes a link and re-clicks it rather than trusting configuration.
breaking_changes.surface: app.cache.spec TTL vs the published takedown bound

breaking_changes.detail: A V1__create_links.sql from a prior run sits on the classpath with no source counterpart. An incremental build applies it, Flyway records its checksum, and the run's own V1 then collides or fails ddl-auto: validate. Because service/target/ is gitignored, nothing in the diff explains the failure.
breaking_changes.mitigation: Run `./mvnw clean verify` (not `verify`) for the first build of this run, or delete service/target before the design node's maven_compiles gate. Owner: whoever kicks off the run; it is a one-line precondition, not a code change.
breaking_changes.surface: Flyway migration history vs stale target/classes

breaking_changes.detail: Compose starts Postgres only. Once the service requires Redis at startup, `docker compose up` yields an application that cannot serve a click, and no pipeline node holds write access to the file to fix it.
breaking_changes.mitigation: A human adds a redis service to docker-compose.yml alongside approving the pom change, in the same review. Tests are unaffected either way because AbstractIntegrationTest uses Testcontainers, not compose - which is what keeps this a developer-experience break rather than a gate failure.

breaking_changes.detail: Not applicable in the usual sense: nothing is deployed and there are no callers, so old and new versions never coexist. The one place the question does bite is inside the build - the greenfield-2/implement branch carries a links schema (hit_count, last_accessed_at, no status column, no customer table) that is not an ancestor of HEAD.
breaking_changes.mitigation: Treat that branch as abandoned rather than as a baseline to migrate from: start migration numbering at V1 on this branch and do not port its SQL. If any of it is reused, it needs re-deriving against A11 soft-delete and A16 ownership, not copying.
breaking_changes.surface: Rolling-deploy compatibility (old vs new running together)

evidence.claim: Adding a Redis CacheManager does NOT create a duplicate-bean failure by itself: Spring Boot's CacheAutoConfiguration is annotated @ConditionalOnMissingBean(value=CacheManager.class, name="cacheResolver") at class level and @AutoConfiguration(after=RedisAutoConfiguration), so the existing CacheConfig.cacheManager bean suppresses all auto-configured cache managers. The break only happens if a node adds a *second* explicit CacheManager bean. Replacing the body of CacheConfig.cacheManager is therefore the safe move.

options.summary: Cache: replace the body of CacheConfig.cacheManager with a RedisCacheManager (keeping the method name and the LINKS_CACHE constant), rather than adding a second cache configuration class. Verified to be conflict-free because Boot's cache auto-config backs off entirely when one CacheManager bean exists.

Cache: two-tier — a small Caffeine near-cache in front of Redis, one bean marked @Primary. Buys a few hundred microseconds on the hottest link (AC22) but reintroduces a per-instance layer that active invalidation cannot reach, so the 60s bound would rest on the near-cache TTL as well.

Auth libraries: take spring-security-crypto (for the KDF) plus jjwt-api/impl/jackson with literal versions, and do NOT take spring-boot-starter-security. Session verification is a plain filter/interceptor, so nothing auto-secures the click path or actuator.

Auth libraries: take spring-boot-starter-security and configure a permitAll SecurityFilterChain for /{code} and /actuator. More idiomatic, but a single missing matcher 401s the public redirect path and breaks AC14, and the failure is a passing build with failing tests.

Rate limiting: hand-roll the token bucket as a Lua script evaluated through the RedisTemplate the Redis starter already provides. No extra dependency, no second supply-chain approval, and single-key operations stay Cluster-safe.

V1 schema: customers, links (domain,code unique; status; expires_at), click totals, abuse reports, threat denylist, seeded customer fixture

JPA entities and repositories matching V1 exactly under ddl-auto: validate
Sign-in endpoint issuing an asymmetrically signed 24h JWT, with Argon2id/BCrypt password verification
Local-only session verification on /api/v1/** with the click path and actuator left unauthenticated
Unguessable short-code generator: 128-bit CSPRNG base62, no derivation from row/time/URL, unique-constraint retry
Create-link endpoint returning code and fully-qualified short URL, with URL validation, threat check and 30-day default expiry
Customer-chosen alias in the shared code namespace: charset and reserved-word rules, 409 on collision with no owner/target disclosure

endpoints.notes: Sign-in. 200 rather than 201: no addressable resource is created, the token is the whole response. Unknown email and wrong password both give 401 invalid_credentials, same body, same timing. 400 malformed, 429 sign-in bucket (per IP). Public (security: []).

Create. Location: /api/v1/links/{code} (the API resource), short URL in the body. 400 syntax/alias-charset/reserved-alias/past-expiry; 401; 409 alias taken (no owner or target disclosed); 422 url_rejected for denylisted, internal or self-referential targets, one message for all three; 429 write bucket; 503 when a create dependency is down - the only place AC20's 'serve clicks over accepting links' is visible on the wire.

Owner-scoped page, filtered in the query not after it. Order fixed at createdAt DESC then code ASC so blind tests have a total order. page>=0, size 1..100, else 400. Includes the caller's expired/deleted/blocked links; never anyone else's.

Performance: durable Postgres total plus un-flushed Redis delta, so the count reflects a click made a second ago. Caller's own expired/deleted/blocked links are visible with retained counts; unknown or another customer's code is 404 with the identical body - never 403, never 410.

Expiry only. Strict bodies make longUrl immutability mechanical: {"longUrl":...} is 400, not a silent no-op. 400 past/absent expiry; 404 not yours; 409 link_not_modifiable when the caller's own link is deleted or blocked (an abuse takedown must not be reversible by its owner); 429.

Soft delete plus active cache invalidation; stops redirecting within the 60s published bound. Idempotent (repeat delete is 204). 204 with no body because a body describing what was deleted confirms what existed. 404 for anything not the caller's.

Blocks the link immediately and records reporter id, timestamp and reason. 202 with no body for ANY syntactically acceptable code whether or not it resolves - a 404 here would be the existence oracle every other endpoint avoids. Authenticated and rate-limited per reporter; that pair is the entire defence against weaponising takedown.

Public redirect. 302 with Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, max-age=0 / Pragma: no-cache / Expires: 0. 404 (identical body and identical cache headers) for unknown, expired, deleted, blocked or malformed codes, and not counted. 429 from the per-IP click bucket or the much tighter not-found bucket. Never 5xx. Must be a bare @GetMapping("/{code}") on a controller with no class-level @RequestMapping.

Served by the same @GetMapping handler - Spring MVC dispatches HEAD to the GET mapping - with identical status and headers and no body. Deliberately NOT a separate operation in openapi.yaml and it must NOT get its own annotation: the routes gate compares documented operations against @Get/@Post/... regex matches, Spring has no @HeadMapping, and a second @RequestMapping in that file would be read as a path prefix and break the route match. Listed here because the behaviour is real, not because a route is missing.

output.rationale:
WHAT IS FROZEN. artifacts/openapi.yaml (8 operations), 25 Java skeletons under service/src/main/java, and service/pom.xml. `mvn -DskipTests compile` passes (BUILD SUCCESS, 27 sources); the OpenAPI passes the lint the gate runs (8 unique operationIds, every operation has responses, all $refs resolve) and contains no match for the no_secrets pattern. The first build of this run was `clean`, which removed the stale target/classes/db/migration/V1__create_links.sql that impact.json flagged.

TWO BLOCKING AMBIGUITIES WERE NEVER ANSWERED BY A HUMAN, AND THIS CONTRACT COMMITS TO A READING OF BOTH. Q1: the published takedown bound is 60 seconds p99 from the delete/report response, delivered by active cache invalidation with app.cache.ttl <= 60s as the floor under it (the scaffold shipped 5 minutes; that alone would breach it by four minutes with nothing failing). If the business's real number is sub-second, the delete and report paths need synchronous multi-tier invalidation and the TTL safety net stops being sufficient - that changes RedirectController, CacheInvalidator and the acceptance test, not the API shape, so the cost of being wrong is contained to one node's worth of rework. Q2: ThreatCheck is a port with a Postgres denylist and a no-op, and it fails open with a WARN when it cannot answer (ThreatVerdict.UNAVAILABLE exists as a third value precisely so a fail-open decision is visible in the logs rather than collapsed into "clean"). If a real reputation feed is expected in this build, the port is where it lands but the work is materially larger and the create path acquires an external latency and procurement dependency. Both readings are the ones clarification proposed; I did not invent a third.

STATUS CODES, ONE AT A TIME. 302 for the redirect, never 301: a 301 is cached indefinitely by default, so the second and later clicks never reach us - that silently breaks the exact click count (AC3), the "no intermediary short-circuit" rule (AC4), delete taking effect (AC8) and the takedown bound (AC9), and none of it would show up in a test of our own service. 307 was rejected only because method preservation buys nothing for browser GETs. 404 and never 410 for expired/deleted links: 410 means "this existed", which distinguishes an expired link from an unissued code and hands an enumerator a free signal; the whole point of A4 is that unknown, expired, deleted, blocked and another customer's code are one indistinguishable answer, byte-for-byte, with the same cache headers. 404 and never 403 for another customer's link, for the same reason - a 403/404 split is an existence oracle and it is the one AC13 and AC15 name. 201 on create with Location pointing at /api/v1/links/{code} rather than at the short URL, because the short URL is pasted, not followed by the client. 204 on delete with no body: a body saying what was deleted is a way to confirm what existed. 202 on abuse report, returned for any well-formed code whether or not it resolves - a 404 there would reintroduce the oracle through the one endpoint that takes a code from an untrusted caller. 409 alias_unavailable for a taken alias (AC6 requires rejection rather than silent reassignment) but 400 for a reserved word, because nobody holds "actuator" and a 409 would imply somebody does. 422 url_rejected, not 400, for a URL that parses but may not be shortened, with one fixed message shared by denylist hits, internal/private/loopback hosts and our own origin, so the response cannot be used to enumerate the denylist or map our network. 401 with a single unauthorized body for every token failure - expired, forged, absent - so a caller cannot learn which tokens are nearly valid. 429 always with Retry-After in whole seconds and never 0. 503 only on create, never on the click path: that asymmetry is AC20's "serve clicks in preference to accepting links" made visible on the wire. 405 for other methods on /{code} comes from Spring's dispatcher and is documented in prose, not as an operation.

CODE LENGTH: A2 IS INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT AND I CORRECTED IT IN THE DIRECTION OF THE ACCEPTANCE CRITERION. A2 says "128 bits of CSPRNG output rendered as ~11 base62 characters"; 11 base62 characters carry ~65 bits, not 128. AC16 is an acceptance criterion and "short" is not, so ShortCodeGenerator.CODE_LENGTH is 22 (ceil(128/log2(62)), ~131 bits) and the reviewer should know the cost: a short link becomes ~40 characters, longer than the products this is modelled on, which buy 7-character codes with aggressive enumeration defence instead. We have that defence too (the separate, much tighter not-found bucket), so trading length against rate limiting later is a one-constant change with no migration - old codes stay valid. If the business would rather have short links than the stated bit strength, this is the line to change, and it should be changed deliberately rather than by an off-by-a-factor-of-two in the assumptions.

OWNER-SCOPED VISIBILITY. A link that is not yours is 404 everywhere. Your own expired, deleted or blocked link is visible on GET with its retained click count, because A11 keeps the row and the count and it is your data; only PATCH refuses it (409 link_not_modifiable), so an abuse takedown cannot be undone by its owner pushing the expiry out. Ownership is filtered in the query, not checked after the fetch - AC13 is an invariant, and a post-fetch comparison is one forgotten branch away from a cross-tenant read.

THE POM: ONE APPROVAL, EVERYTHING IT NEEDS. spring-boot-starter-data-redis (BOM-managed) for click counters, the resolution cache with negative caching, and the token buckets - a per-instance cache cannot be actively invalidated, which would leave the 60s bound resting on TTL alone, and a per-instance limiter multiplies every limit by the replica count. spring-security-crypto for the KDF and deliberately NOT spring-boot-starter-security: the starter's auto-configured filter chain covers every mapping including the root redirect, and one missing matcher 401s the public click path (AC14) with a green build. bcprov-jdk18on:1.81 pinned explicitly - Argon2PasswordEncoder references org/bouncycastle but spring-security-crypto declares no such dependency, so without this pin the service compiles, passes every gate and throws NoClassDefFoundError at the first sign-in; this is U4, and since neither downstream branch may edit pom.xml it had to be decided here. If the approver rejects the extra supply-chain entry, A6's sanctioned fallback is BCrypt cost 12, self-contained in the same jar - but that is the approver's call, not implement's. jjwt-api/impl/jackson 0.12.6 with literal versions because Boot's BOM manages no JWT version (verified: zero matches for nimbus/jjwt/bouncycastle in spring-boot-dependencies-3.5.16). Rate limiting is a hand-written Lua script over the existing Redis connection rather than a bucket library: no second supply-chain approval, and single-key operations stay Cluster-safe against the unresolved U1. org.testcontainers:testcontainers declared explicitly (test scope) so the harness can use GenericContainer for Redis without leaning on another module's transitive graph; spring-boot-testcontainers already ships the Redis @ServiceConnection factory, so no third-party Redis module is needed. Caffeine is retained only because the scaffold's CacheConfig still builds a CaffeineCacheManager; the contract states that implement replaces the body of that one bean method rather than adding a second CacheManager (two candidates fail context load for every integration test at once and read like a broken harness) and that a Caffeine near-cache is out, because active invalidation cannot reach a per-instance tier. All new coordinates were resolved from Maven Central during the compile, so they exist at the versions pinned.

THE CONFIG SURFACE IS FROZEN AS A TYPE, NOT LEFT TO application.yml. application.yml is not in this node's write paths, so AppProperties is the only way the two branches can agree on configuration: implement reads these keys, and author-tests - which never sees application.yml - needs the property names to drive a bucket down to a testable size via @SpringBootTest(properties=...). Every key has a default here, so a key missing from application.yml degrades to this file rather than failing to bind. Rate-limit defaults are production defaults chosen high enough that an ordinary suite running from 127.0.0.1 does not self-throttle; the not-found bucket is an order of magnitude tighter than the click bucket, because an enumeration sweep is a run of 404s while a viral link is a run of 302s and AC22 requires the second to survive whatever we do to the first. A SIGN_IN bucket was added beyond A13's three: an unthrottled sign-in is an open credential-stuffing target, and AC17's promise about stolen databases is worth little if passwords can be guessed at the front door.

FIXTURES ARE PART OF THE FREEZE. There is no registration endpoint, so the two seeded customers (alice@example.com / bob@example.com, fixed UUIDs, plaintexts in the spec) and the two denylisted hosts (malware.example.com, phishing.example.net, both in reserved example space so nothing real is implicated) are written into openapi.yaml. Without them the migration and the tests would each invent their own and every auth and AC21 test would fail at the join for a reason that looks like a bug. Two customers, because tenant isolation cannot be tested with one. The migration stores an Argon2id hash, never the plaintext, and credentials in configuration keep the existing unquoted ${VAR:default} style so the no_secrets gate does not fire on a false positive.

GATE-SHAPED CONSTRAINTS STATED IN THE CONTRACT RATHER THAN DISCOVERED AT VERIFY. routes_match_openapi is a regex over Spring annotations, so: HEAD /{code} is not a documented operation and must not get its own mapping (Spring has no @HeadMapping and a stray @RequestMapping in that file would be parsed as a path prefix); the redirect controller must carry a bare @GetMapping("/{code}") with no class-level @RequestMapping; actuator endpoints are not documented because they are not @*Mapping annotations and documenting them would fail the same gate. Strict request bodies (unknown property -> 400) need spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties: true in application.yml; that is what makes longUrl immutability mechanical rather than a silently ignored field.

UNKNOWNS I DESIGNED PAST, AND THE READING TAKEN. U1 (Redis topology): assumed single instance/Sentinel, AOF, no eviction; every Redis operation in this design is single-key or hash-taggable so a Cluster move stays additive, but if the shared Redis runs allkeys-lru a counter key can be evicted before flush and clicks are lost against AC3 with no error anywhere - that is a question for the platform owner, not something a test here can catch. U5 (JWT key provenance): keys come from the environment as PEM placeholders; when both are blank the service generates an ephemeral keypair and logs a warning, which is correct for one instance and for tests and wrong for replicas, where a token issued by one instance will not verify on another - AppProperties.Session says so in its javadoc so the trap is documented where someone will read it. U6 (Redis down at startup): the service starts and serves redirects from PostgreSQL with counting degraded; Lettuce connects lazily, so this costs nothing and it is the only reading consistent with AC20. U7 (denylist writes): seeded by migration plus the abuse-report path; there is no admin endpoint, so marking a URL bad in production is currently a migration under an approval gate - a real operational gap, flagged rather than solved, because an admin API is a surface nobody asked for.

KNOWN, ACCEPTED HOLE. The alias path is an existence oracle by construction: create-with-alias answers 409 when the code is taken, so a caller can probe any code for existence. It cannot be closed without breaking AC5/AC6, and it is worthless against generated codes at 128 bits; the per-customer write bucket and the requirement of a signed-in session bound it. Stated here because a security reviewer will find it and should find our reasoning next to it.

DELIBERATELY NOT DONE. No controllers (implement's job; the contract fixes their routes instead), no application.yml or migrations (not in this node's write paths), and no docker-compose.yml - it is in no node's write paths and still defines Postgres only, so the human approving this pom should add a redis service in the same review or `docker compose up` yields a service that cannot serve a click, invisibly to every mechanical gate.

findings.suggestion: Batch the durable writes: one transaction per pass with a multi-row update (or a JDBC batch of `update links set click_count = click_count + ? where id = ?`) instead of one transaction per link, and pipeline the settle decrements. Then raise flush-batch-size and measure drain rate against arrival rate. To confirm before shipping: expose `HLEN clicks:pending` as a gauge and alert if it trends upward — a monotonically growing pending hash is the signal that the drain is behind, and it is currently invisible.
findings.summary: The click drain has a hard throughput ceiling of 500 distinct links per 5s pass (app.click.flush-batch-size=500, flush-interval=PT5S), and each link costs one JPA transaction plus one Redis settle round trip, executed sequentially on a single scheduler thread. That is ~100 links/second per instance. Above that arrival rate of *distinct* clicked links, the Redis pending hash grows without bound: nothing ever removes fields faster than they are added, and the backlog is what feeds PERF-2. The service's stated scale (A2 reasons about 100M links/day) is three to four orders of magnitude above this ceiling. Every instance runs the same unsharded schedule, so adding replicas multiplies the read of the same hash rather than dividing the work.

findings.suggestion: Replace HGETALL with a cursor: `HSCAN key cursor COUNT n` in a loop inside the script until `limit` fields are collected, persisting the cursor (or using a per-pass random start) so passes make progress across the hash. The zero-field sweep can stay on the scanned window. To confirm: `redis-cli --latency` and the `latency history command` event, or SLOWLOG, during a pass with a synthetically large pending hash.
findings.summary: readPending bounds what it *returns* (limit) but not what it *reads*: the script calls HGETALL on the entire pending hash and then discards everything past the limit. The batch is therefore not bounded at all in cost — it is O(total pending links) in Redis CPU and in Lua-side memory, every 5 seconds, on every instance. Redis executes scripts single-threaded, so a pass over a hash that has grown to hundreds of thousands of fields (see PERF-1) blocks the same Redis instance that serves the resolution cache and the rate limiter on the redirect hot path. The failure couples: a click-counting backlog becomes redirect latency, and the 1s command timeout then converts it into cache misses and fail-open rate limiting rather than an outage — but it is the hot path degrading because of a background job.

findings.suggestion: Fetch all pending deltas for the page in one call: `opsForHash().multiGet(pendingKey, codes)` (HMGET is single-key, so it keeps the Cluster-safety property the class documents), and do it after the transaction returns rather than inside it. The same fix applies to reading the delta once per page instead of once per row.
findings.summary: GET /api/v1/links maps every row through toResponse, which calls clickCounter.pendingDelta per link — one Redis HGET per item, sequential, up to 100 per request (MAX_PAGE_SIZE). This is a textbook N+1 against the cache tier, and it happens inside a readOnly @Transactional that has already acquired a Hibernate connection for the page query, so a Hikari connection is pinned for the whole串 of Redis round trips. With the configured 1s Redis timeout, a degraded-but-alive Redis makes one list request occupy a database connection for up to 100 seconds; ten such requests exhaust the default pool of 10 and stall every other endpoint, including a redirect that missed cache.

findings.suggestion: Drop @Transactional from resolve() and let the repository call use its own transaction, then perform cache.put after it returns. Confirm with a connection-hold histogram (Hikari `hikaricp.connections.usage` is already exported via the Prometheus registry) comparing hit and miss requests.
findings.summary: resolve() is @Transactional(readOnly = true) and the cache write (cache.put, a Redis round trip) happens inside that transaction, after the JDBC statement has acquired a connection. Hibernate's delayed acquisition means a cache *hit* costs no connection — good — but every *miss* holds a pooled connection across a Redis PUT with a 1s timeout. Under a miss storm (see PERF-5) that is connection-hold time proportional to Redis latency rather than to database latency, on the one path that must not queue. The transaction also buys nothing here: it wraps a single read.

findings.suggestion: Set spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size explicitly with a comment tying it to expected concurrency and PostgreSQL max_connections, and consider per-code single-flight (a striped lock or Caffeine-style loading wrapper around the miss path) so a hot link's TTL expiry produces one database read rather than one per in-flight click. Measure: hikaricp.connections.pending and the redirect miss ratio under a sustained load test.
findings.summary: No connection pool sizing is configured, so Hikari runs at its default maximum of 10 connections, and nothing configures the Lettuce or Tomcat side either. That interacts with a structural property of the design: app.cache.ttl is pinned at 60s to floor the takedown bound, so every actively-clicked link must be re-read from PostgreSQL at least once per minute per replica, and there is no single-flight — N concurrent clicks arriving on a link whose entry has just expired all miss and all issue the same lookup. The redirect's database read rate therefore has a floor of (distinct active links)/60s, served through 10 connections. It is an indexed unique lookup on ux_links_domain_code so each is cheap, but the pool, not the query, is the ceiling, and nobody has picked the number deliberately.

findings.suggestion: Reject anything failing `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,64}$` at the top of follow() with the same notFound() response (identical body and headers, so it stays indistinguishable), before touching the cache or the database. This costs nothing and removes both the Redis key-space and the database round trip for malformed codes.
findings.summary: The redirect accepts any path segment as a code with no length or charset bound before spending work on it. AliasPolicy caps codes at 64 characters and the column is VARCHAR(64), yet a multi-kilobyte path still becomes a Redis GET key, a PostgreSQL query parameter, and — on a miss — a negatively-cached Redis entry keyed by the full garbage string. Cost per request is small and 60s TTLs bound the memory, but it is work and cache space an attacker chooses the size of, on the one endpoint that is unauthenticated and rate-limited only per-IP.

findings.suggestion: If the totals must stay in the contract, at least bound `page` (or cap offset) the way `size` is capped in requireValidPaging. Longer term, keyset pagination on (created_at desc, code asc) removes both the count and the offset walk. Confirm with EXPLAIN ANALYZE of the count query against a customer with ~1M links.
findings.summary: findOwnedBy returns Page, so Spring Data issues a `select count(...)` alongside every list request, and LinkPage exposes totalElements/totalPages so it cannot be dropped without an API change. The count scans the whole customer_id range of ix_links_owner_listing on every page request — for a customer with a large link inventory that is the expensive half of the request, repeated for each page. Offset paging compounds it: `page` is unbounded, so page=100000 makes PostgreSQL walk and discard the offset rows. This is a management endpoint, not the hot path, so the blast radius is one caller's latency and the connection they hold.

findings.suggestion: Bound password hashing with a semaphore (or a small dedicated executor) sized to available cores, returning 503/429 when saturated, so credential-stuffing load cannot displace the redirect path. Measure: heap allocation rate and p99 redirect latency while replaying concurrent sign-in failures.
findings.summary: Every sign-in attempt — including every failed one, deliberately, for timing-equality — runs Argon2id at m=16384 KiB, t=2. Nothing bounds how many run concurrently: Tomcat's default 200 request threads means up to 200 simultaneous hashes, ~3.2 GiB of transient heap allocation and full CPU saturation, from unauthenticated requests. The sign-in bucket (60/min/IP) is the only brake and it fails open when Redis is unreachable, which is precisely when the service is already unhappy. Cost of being wrong is a GC-thrashing JVM that also stops serving redirects, since they share the same thread pool and heap.

findings.suggestion: Two cheap options that keep the exactness guarantee: pipeline the rate-limit and cache-GET into one round trip (both are needed unconditionally), and/or issue the HINCRBY asynchronously on the Lettuce connection without awaiting the reply, so the 302 is not gated on it — this differs from the executor-with-a-queue the javadoc rightly rejects, since it drops nothing. At minimum, lower the Redis command timeout for the increment specifically, and measure the redirect p99 with a latency-injected Redis (`CLIENT PAUSE` or a toxiproxy) to see the tail the current arrangement produces.
findings.summary: The analytics write is on the critical path, and this is a documented deliberate trade (ClickCounter's javadoc, AC3) rather than an oversight — but the shape is worth stating plainly: a served redirect makes three *sequential* Redis round trips (rate-limit script, cache GET, click HINCRBY) before the 302 is written, four on a not-found. Each carries the 1s command timeout, so a Redis that is slow rather than down can add up to ~3s to a redirect that would otherwise be served entirely from cached data. The increment in particular delays the response purely to record a statistic.

findings.suggestion: Either store and query email lower-cased (as threat_denylist.host already does, with the comment explaining exactly this reasoning), or add `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_customers_email_lower ON customers (lower(email))` and query with a matching predicate. Confirm with EXPLAIN on the generated statement.
findings.summary: findByEmailIgnoreCase generates `upper(email) = upper(?)`, which cannot use the ux_customers_email btree index in V1__initial_schema.sql — every sign-in is a sequential scan of customers. Today that is two seeded rows and there is no registration endpoint, so the cost is nil; it is filed only because the index exists and reads as if it serves this lookup, and the day accounts arrive the scan arrives with them.

not_examined: Actual query plans — no database was available to me, so index usability is inferred from the migration DDL and the derived-query naming, not from EXPLAIN output.
JVM heap sizing, GC behaviour and allocation rates; the Argon2 memory arithmetic in PERF-8 is from the encoder's documented parameters, not measured.
Ed25519 JWT verification cost per management request (JwtVerifier/jjwt+BouncyCastle) — it is off the redirect path and I did not benchmark it.

Lettuce connection multiplexing behaviour under saturation: I assumed the shared non-pooled connection the Redis starter configures by default and did not verify how it queues commands when Redis is slow.

Tomcat thread pool, request body size caps and max-http-request-header sizes — all left at Spring Boot defaults, none configured in application.yml, and I did not trace what those defaults are in Boot 3.5.16.

Redis deployment topology, memory limits and eviction policy (docker-compose.yml read only for pool/limit settings) — whether the cache tier is allowed to evict under pressure decides what PERF-2's growing hash actually does.
The test suite's own runtime and Testcontainers behaviour; the build is reported green and I did not run it.

Behaviour of the flush job with more than one replica beyond what RedisClickCounter's javadoc asserts — I took the non-destructive read/settle invariant on trust rather than reasoning through every interleaving.
Anything requiring a profiler: allocation hot spots, serialization cost of Jackson2JsonRedisSerializer per cache read on the redirect path, and actual per-request CPU.
output.summary: The core hot path is well built: the redirect is a single indexed (domain, code) lookup behind a Redis cache that also caches misses, clicks never touch PostgreSQL synchronously, the rate limiter is one atomic single-key Lua call that fails open, and both the unique constraint and the concurrent-alias race are handled correctly. At the load this service will plausibly see on day one, the redirect is fine. The problems are all in the machinery around it, and two are structural rather than micro. First, the click drain cannot keep up by construction: 500 links per 5s pass, one transaction and one Redis round trip each, means ~100 distinct links/second per instance against a design that reasons about 100M links/day — the pending hash only grows. Second, the drain reads that hash with HGETALL and discards everything past the limit, so the batch bounds output but not cost; a backlog therefore turns into a single-threaded Redis stall every 5 seconds, on the same Redis the redirect depends on. Those two compound each other and are the findings worth acting on. Third and independent: the list endpoint does one Redis HGET per row inside a transaction holding a database connection, which is an N+1 that pins a pool connection for up to 100 sequential Redis timeouts. The remainder are smaller — an unsized connection pool under a cache TTL that is pinned at 60s by the takedown bound (so database read rate has a floor and there is no single-flight on a miss), an unbounded code length reaching the cache and database, count-plus-offset paging, unbounded concurrent Argon2 hashing, and a non-indexable email lookup that costs nothing today. I could not measure any of this; the severities reflect mechanisms I can read in the code, and I have said where I am extrapolating to load nobody has run.

findings.suggestion: The code is wrong. Either reject a code longer than the CodePath maxLength of 64 with the documented 400 (invalid_request) before the insert, or truncate/store it as text; do not let a database constraint decide the status. Keep answering 202 for any code within the documented length so the endpoint stays a non-oracle.
findings.summary: POST /api/v1/links/{code}/abuse-reports accepts a path code of any length and inserts it into abuse_reports.code, declared VARCHAR(64) in V1__initial_schema.sql:47. A code longer than 64 characters makes Postgres raise a length error, Hibernate wraps it as DataIntegrityViolationException, and nothing handles it: the caller gets 500 with Spring Boot's default error body ({"timestamp","status","error","path"}). The spec (openapi.yaml:563-573) documents only 202/400/401/429 for this operation, and openapi.yaml:47 says every non-2xx body has the ApiError shape. This is the one endpoint that takes an unvalidated code from an untrusted caller and writes it, so it is the reachable case.

findings.suggestion: The code is wrong. Add a fallback @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) that logs and returns a fixed ApiError body; then either document a 500 entry in the error catalogue or map the reachable dependency failures onto the statuses that are documented (see API-3). The click path already does this deliberately (RedirectController:86) - the management path does not.
findings.summary: ApiExceptionHandler covers ApiException, MethodArgumentNotValid, HttpMessageNotReadable, MethodArgumentTypeMismatch and MissingServletRequestParameter, and nothing else. Any other RuntimeException on the management surface (a Postgres outage mid-request, a Jackson serialization failure, the DataIntegrityViolation of API-1) falls through to Boot's BasicErrorController, which answers 500 with {"timestamp","status","error","path"} - not ApiError. openapi.yaml:47 states the catalogue is closed and every non-2xx body has the ApiError shape; 500 appears nowhere in the document. This is the framework default leaking through at the one point nobody decided.

findings.suggestion: The code is wrong. Map DataAccessResourceFailureException/CannotCreateTransactionException on the create path onto ApiException.dependencyUnavailable so the documented 503 is what a caller actually sees; alternatively document that 503 covers only the cache and threat tiers, which would be a weaker promise than openapi.yaml:325 currently makes.
findings.summary: openapi.yaml:324-337 documents 503 service_unavailable on POST /api/v1/links for "a dependency the create path needs is unavailable". In the code, 503 is produced in exactly three places: short-code exhaustion (LinkService:182), the threat checker being unavailable with fail-open disabled (LinkService:198, and fail-open is true by default), and the resolution cache being unreachable before issuing (ResolutionCache:91). The dependency most likely to be unavailable - PostgreSQL - is not one of them: saveAndFlush throws a DataAccessException, which reaches no handler and answers 500 with the framework body. The documented degradation story for AC20 therefore does not hold for the most probable outage.

findings.suggestion: Decide and record which side moves. Either set spring.mvc.throw-exception-if-no-handler-found and handle NoResourceFoundException/HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException into ApiError, or state in the spec that dispatcher-level 404/405 responses carry the container's body and are outside the closed catalogue.
findings.summary: Dispatcher-level refusals on the management surface return the framework error body rather than ApiError: an unknown path under /api/v1 with a valid token (NoResourceFoundException -> 404) and a wrong method on a documented path (e.g. PUT /api/v1/links/{code} -> 405). openapi.yaml:29-43 promises the not-found body byte for byte "on both surfaces", and openapi.yaml:47 promises the ApiError shape for every non-2xx. Note 2 (openapi.yaml:123) exempts only the /{code} 405 status, not the body shape, and says nothing about the management surface.

findings.suggestion: Document the actuator surface in the spec (or a note stating it is operational and not part of the public contract), and consider narrowing exposure to health,info - metrics and prometheus unauthenticated is a decision the release gate should take knowingly rather than inherit from a config line.
findings.summary: management.endpoints.web.exposure.include exposes /actuator/health, /actuator/info, /actuator/metrics and /actuator/prometheus. These are outside the session filter (WebConfig:28 registers it for /api/v1/* only), so they are unauthenticated, and they appear nowhere in openapi.yaml, whose "Two surfaces" table (openapi.yaml:18-21) lists only the management API and the click path. The spec acknowledges actuator exists only obliquely, in the reserved-alias rationale. Undocumented surface becomes a de facto contract as soon as a caller or a probe depends on it - and metrics/prometheus is more than a liveness probe.

findings.suggestion: Decide which side is right and write it down. If BLOCKED must survive a delete, make markDeleted conditional the way markBlocked is and keep answering 204 (idempotent, no new status). If an owner may relabel their blocked link, say so in the DELETE description, because a reader of the PATCH 409 rationale will assume the opposite.
findings.summary: DELETE on the caller's own BLOCKED link answers 204 and overwrites the status to DELETED (LinkService:141 -> markDeleted, which is unconditional, unlike markBlocked at LinkEntity:139 which deliberately refuses to overwrite). The spec documents 409 link_not_modifiable for PATCH on a deleted or blocked link (openapi.yaml:487-498) on the reasoning that a link taken down for abuse is no longer the owner's to change, but DELETE documents no 409 (openapi.yaml:518-528), so 204 conforms on status. The divergence is in the representation: after this, GET /api/v1/links/{code} reports status DELETED for a link that was taken down for abuse, and the takedown is invisible in the API.

findings.suggestion: Add spring.jackson.serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps: false explicitly, next to the deserialization block that is already pinned for the same reason.
findings.summary: The spec freezes the timestamp format (openapi.yaml:67, ISO-8601 instants in UTC) and the config pins fail-on-unknown-properties for the strict-body rule right beside it, but nothing pins serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps. The contract-correct rendering of createdAt/expiresAt therefore rests on Spring Boot's default of disabling that feature. The default is currently right - Instant renders as 2026-08-10T12:00:00Z - so this is not a live divergence, only an unpinned one on a value the spec calls frozen.

findings.suggestion: No code change implied by the contract. Consider a sentence in the /{code} 404 description recording that an internal failure is also answered this way, so the 404 is not read as a positive assertion that the code was never issued.
findings.summary: The click path catches every RuntimeException and answers the documented 404 not_found. That honours "this operation never returns 5xx" (openapi.yaml:601), and the 404 body and cache headers match the spec exactly - but it means a PostgreSQL outage renders every live link as "does not resolve", which is indistinguishable to a caller from mass deletion. The contract offers no other status, so the code is following it; the consequence is worth a reviewer's eye rather than a change.

output.summary: The implementation honours the contract on every happy path and on almost every documented error. All eight routes match the spec's eight operations exactly, with no undocumented controller mapping. Statuses are right where they matter most: 302 (not 301) on the redirect with Location set verbatim and the pinned no-store/Pragma/Expires headers; 201 with a relative Location of /api/v1/links/{code}; 204 with no body on delete; 202 with no body and no existence signal on abuse report; 200 on sign-in. The single-404 rule holds - unknown, expired, deleted, blocked and other-customer codes all reach ApiException.notFound() or ApiError.NOT_FOUND, with fields omitted via @JsonInclude(NON_NULL), so the body is byte-identical on both surfaces, and there is no 403 or 410 anywhere. Response DTOs carry exactly the documented fields with the documented names and types (no extras, nothing renamed), the strict-body rule is genuinely enforced (spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties: true, so PATCH {"longUrl":...} is a 400), the 400/422 split between URL syntax and host policy is implemented as described, reserved aliases are 400 and taken aliases 409, Retry-After is rounded up and floored at 1, and the seeded fixtures match the freeze. Where it diverges is the failure paths nobody decided. There is no fallback exception handler, so any unexpected RuntimeException on the management surface answers 500 with Spring Boot's default error body rather than the ApiError shape the spec calls closed (API-2). That is concretely reachable: an abuse report against a code longer than 64 characters violates a VARCHAR(64) column and returns that 500 instead of a documented status (API-1). And the create path's documented 503 covers the cache, the threat checker and code exhaustion but not a database outage, which is the dependency failure the AC20 sentence most obviously means (API-3). Those three are where the contract breaks; the rest are documentation gaps (undocumented actuator surface, dispatcher-level 404/405 bodies) and one behavioural question about deleting a blocked link.

findings.suggestion: Make the configured value load-bearing or delete it. Cheapest consistent option: have `LinkPolicyConfig.urlValidator(...)` pass `properties.links().maxUrlLength()` into `UrlValidator` (it already passes `baseUrl`), and drop the now-redundant hardcoded constant; keep `@Size(max = 2048)` only if you reference a shared constant, since a bean-validation annotation needs a compile-time constant.
findings.summary: The maximum long-URL length exists three times and only two of them agree by accident: `UrlValidator.MAX_URL_LENGTH = 2048`, `@Size(max = 2048)` on `CreateLinkRequest.longUrl` (line 25), and `app.links.max-url-length: 2048` in application.yml bound to `AppProperties.Links.maxUrlLength` — which no code reads. Raising the limit in config changes nothing, and a reviewer would reasonably believe it did.

findings.suggestion: Write `@Pattern(regexp = AliasPolicy.PATTERN)` — it is a `public static final String`, so it is a valid annotation constant — and delete the comment. If a package cycle is unwanted, move `PATTERN` to the `api` package and have `AliasPolicy` reference it.
findings.summary: The alias charset rule is a literal regex on the DTO and again as `AliasPolicy.PATTERN`. `AliasPolicy` even carries the comment "identical to the one on the request DTO", which documents the drift risk rather than removing it — and `PATTERN` also duplicates `MIN_LENGTH`/`MAX_LENGTH` inside its own literal.

findings.suggestion: Drop the inline default — `@Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "${app.click.flush-interval}")` — since `@DefaultValue("PT5S")` plus application.yml already supply it, and add a one-line comment on `AppProperties.Click.flushInterval` saying it is consumed by the annotation rather than by a constructor, so the accessor does not read as dead.
findings.summary: `@Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "${app.click.flush-interval:PT5S}")` reaches past the typed configuration surface that the rest of the change uses uniformly (`AppProperties`), and restates the PT5S default that `AppProperties.Click.flushInterval` already declares. `AppProperties.Click.flushInterval()` is consequently read by nothing, so the documented accessor and the actual schedule can diverge silently.

findings.suggestion: Delete the unused `LinkEntity.isResolvableAt` and have `CachedLink.redirectsAt` be the single statement of the rule, or express both in terms of one static predicate on `LinkStatus`. Whichever way, one of the two should stop existing.
findings.summary: "A link redirects when it is ACTIVE and not yet expired" is expressed twice: `CachedLink.redirectsAt` and `LinkEntity.statusAt`/`isResolvableAt`. They must agree — adding a fourth `LinkStatus` or changing the expiry boundary from exclusive to inclusive has to be done in both — and `LinkEntity.isResolvableAt` is currently called by nothing, so nothing would fail if only one copy were updated.

findings.suggestion: Move the container-independent helpers to static methods on `ApiClient` or `Fixtures` (e.g. `Fixtures.givenLink(api, bearer)`, `ApiClient.clickRepeatedly(api, code, times)`) and have both base classes delegate, so the restart harness inherits nothing but still shares one definition of each helper.
findings.summary: `alice()`, `bob()`, `givenLink(bearer)`, `sleep(Duration)` and `clickRepeatedly(...)` are re-implemented here alongside `AbstractIntegrationTest`. The class comment explains convincingly why the two cannot share a superclass, but that argument does not extend to the helpers themselves — and `clickRepeatedly` has already drifted: it returns `List<Integer>` here and `List<HttpResponse<String>>` there, so the same name means two things depending on which base class a test extends.

findings.suggestion: Update §7 to match the delivered contract (or mark it superseded by artifacts/design.json), and change the `CacheConfig` javadoc to point at something that exists — the negative-caching rationale is already written in `LinkResolver` and `CachedLink`.
findings.summary: §7 of the committed "plan of record" now contradicts the service that was built: it states 410-for-expired vs 404-for-unknown (the design deliberately chose 404 for both), "Caffeine only — no Redis in the build" (the change is Redis-backed throughout), a `/api/v1/links/{code}/stats` endpoint, `Idempotency-Key`, an outbox, and 7-character codes (shipped: 22). Relatedly, `CacheConfig.LINKS_CACHE` cites "the enumeration note in ADR-004", but no ADR documents exist in the repo and the only ADR-004 reference is this plan's 7-character code decision.

findings.suggestion: Either drop the ones with no caller, or add a single line to each saying it is contract surface retained for future callers, so a later reader does not have to grep the whole repo to find out.
findings.summary: A handful of members exist for tests that never call them: `UrlValidator.ownHost()` and its no-arg constructor, `ShortCodeGenerator.random()` and its `SecureRandom` constructor, `RateLimitDecision.remaining()`, `LinkEntity.getDomain()`/`getCustomerId()`. They were plausibly frozen into the contract before the tests were written, which is a real reason — but as shipped they are surface nobody exercises.

findings.suggestion: Replace `\'` with `'` in the three AbuseReportService javadoc lines, and add the `java.util.UUID` import in `SignInService`.
findings.summary: Javadoc contains escaped apostrophes (`competitor\'s`, `customer\'s` on lines 35 and 36) — a shell-escaping artifact that renders literally in the generated docs. Separately, `SignInService.java:46` writes `java.util.UUID.randomUUID()` fully qualified where every other file in the change imports `java.util.UUID`.
