output.summary: This is unusually clean, consistent code for a greenfield change of this size: one naming vocabulary, one error catalogue, business rules in the service layer with the controllers doing routing and rate-limit charging only, no swallowed exceptions that are not explicitly argued for (every `catch (RuntimeException)` here is a documented fail-open with a log line at a defensible level, and the fail-open decisions log loudly enough to diagnose from), and comments that overwhelmingly explain *why* rather than *what*. Nothing I found is close to a blocker. The findings that will cost someone real time are duplications that must stay in agreement and have no mechanism keeping them so: the max-URL-length rule in three places with the configured copy dead (CLEAN-1), the alias regex literal duplicated with a comment acknowledging it (CLEAN-2), the flush interval bypassing the typed config surface everything else uses (CLEAN-3), the redirect-eligibility rule in two classes (CLEAN-4), and already-drifted helpers across the two test base classes (CLEAN-5). CLEAN-6 is documentation the change left contradicting the code. The remaining nits are few on purpose; other minor things I saw and did not file — near-verbatim rationale paragraphs repeated between `RateLimiter` and `RedisTokenBucketRateLimiter`, and between `RateLimitDecision.ALLOWED` and its implementation, plus `ThreatCheckConfig` living in `threat` while the other three `@Configuration` classes live in `config` — are minor and internally consistent.

findings.suggestion: Move the two customer INSERTs into a separate location (e.g. `classpath:db/testdata`) added to `spring.flyway.locations` only under a dev/test profile, leaving the denylist rows in the main migration. Provision real accounts by an operator step. Then rotate the plaintexts out of openapi.yaml, or mark them clearly as fixtures that exist only when the test location is active.
findings.summary: Two customer accounts with published plaintext passwords are seeded by an ordinary Flyway migration that runs in every environment. artifacts/openapi.yaml lines 99-102 publish `alice-dev-password` / `bob-dev-password`, and the migration comment claims the accounts are "for local and test use only" — but nothing enforces that: application.yml sets `spring.flyway.enabled: true` with `locations: classpath:db/migration` and no profile or placeholder gate, so a production deploy installs both accounts. Since there is no registration endpoint, these are the accounts, and either one can create links, and — via the abuse endpoint — take down any link on the service (see SEC-5).

findings.suggestion: Normalise the host once in `UrlValidator.parseOrThrow` — lower-case, strip trailing dots, reject empty labels — and check and store that normalised form, so the denylist, the own-host check and the stored target all agree. Add a test asserting `https://malware.example.com./x` and `https://MALWARE.example.com/x` are both refused with the same 422 body as the plain form.
findings.summary: Denylist bypass by trailing-dot FQDN. `URI.getHost()` on `https://malware.example.com./campaign` returns `malware.example.com.` (verified on JDK 21); the check lower-cases but does not strip the root dot, so `existsByHost` misses, and the parent walk yields `example.com.`, `com.`, `` — never the listed `malware.example.com`. The link is created and redirects, and every browser and resolver treats the trailing dot as the same name. This defeats AC21 on the create path with a one-character change to the submitted URL.

findings.suggestion: Either set `server.forward-headers-strategy: native|framework` and have the edge overwrite (not append to) `X-Forwarded-For` so the app sees a trustworthy client address, or state in the contract that the edge owns per-IP limiting and drop the app-side IP buckets. Do not read `X-Forwarded-For` directly without a trusted-proxy list — that turns the limit into something the attacker chooses. A test that drives two requests with different forwarded addresses through one socket would pin whichever choice is made.
findings.summary: The three buckets the contract documents as "keyed by client IP" (click, not-found, sign-in) are keyed by `request.getRemoteAddr()`, and nothing sets `server.forward-headers-strategy` in application.yml. Behind any load balancer or edge proxy that is the proxy's address for every request, so all callers share one bucket. Two consequences, both bad: per-source throttling for AC19 does not distinguish sources at all, and the global caps become a self-inflicted denial of service — 3000 clicks/min and 60 sign-ins/min for the entire service, against a stated target of ~100M clicks/day. Same call at SignInController.java:40.

findings.suggestion: Make the failure mode per bucket: keep fail-open for CLICK (that rationale is sound and AC20 asks for it), and fail closed — or fall back to a small in-process bucket per instance — for SIGN_IN, WRITE and ABUSE_REPORT, where refusing is the safe direction. Add a bounded concurrency limit around password verification so sign-in cannot consume the whole heap regardless of the limiter's state, and a test that asserts sign-in is still throttled with the Redis container stopped.
findings.summary: The limiter fails open for every bucket, not just the click path it is justified for. When Redis is unreachable the sign-in bucket also allows everything, so a Redis outage removes all brute-force and credential-stuffing protection at the same moment, and lets an unauthenticated caller drive unbounded memory-hard Argon2id work (16 MiB per attempt) against the service. The same outage removes the only bound on abuse-report takedowns and on junk-link creation. Note the outage need not be an accident — the click path itself is the cheapest way to pressure the shared Redis.

findings.suggestion: Add a per-reporter daily cap distinct from the per-minute bucket, and require either a second distinct reporter or an operator confirmation before blocking a link above a click threshold (the high-traffic links are exactly the ones worth attacking). Independently, add an operator-only unblock path so an incorrect takedown is recoverable; the audit rows already record who reported what.
findings.summary: Any signed-in customer can permanently disable any link whose code they have seen, and short codes are seen by everyone who is handed the link. The takedown is immediate, and it is irreversible in this build: `LinkService.updateExpiry` answers 409 for a non-ACTIVE link and there is no unblock path, so a false or malicious takedown is unrecoverable without a DBA. Clarification Q4 accepted the mechanism on the strength of "rate-limited per reporter" plus an audit row, but the limit chosen is 60/min — 86,400 links a day from one account — which does not bound the attack the design said it bounded, and the accepted reasoning did not consider irreversibility.

findings.suggestion: Treat any host containing no alphabetic character as an address literal and run it through `InetAddress.getByName` before `isInternalAddress`, which covers decimal, octal and short-form IPv4 in one line. The DNS-name case is already documented as deliberately out of scope and can stay that way.
findings.summary: The loopback/private/link-local target check is bypassable with non-dotted-quad address literals. `IPV4_LITERAL` matches only `d.d.d.d`, so `isIpLiteral` returns false for `http://2130706433/` and `http://0/`, they are treated as ordinary names, and `InetAddress` is never consulted — verified on JDK 21 that `getByName("2130706433")` is 127.0.0.1 and `getByName("0")` is 0.0.0.0. Impact is bounded because nothing fetches the target server-side, so this is not SSRF; it is the shortener being usable to point clickers at loopback and LAN addresses under our name, which is the case the 422 rule exists to prevent.

findings.suggestion: Reject codes that cannot exist before touching the cache or the database: length 1..64 and charset `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`. On the click path answer the standard 404 (no cache write, no query); on the abuse path answer the standard 202 without writing a row, so neither response becomes an oracle. A test posting a 200-character code to the abuse endpoint would have caught the 500.
findings.summary: The `{code}` path variable is never validated for shape or length on either untrusted path. On the abuse endpoint it is persisted straight into `abuse_reports.code VARCHAR(64)`, so a code longer than 64 characters raises DataIntegrityViolationException, which no handler in ApiExceptionHandler catches — the caller gets a 500 where the contract promises a uniform 202, turning an untrusted input into an unhandled server error. On the click path an arbitrarily long code becomes a Redis negative-cache key, letting a caller burn shared Redis memory with entries that can never correspond to a real link.

findings.suggestion: Bind actuator to a separate management port on the internal interface (`management.server.port`), or expose only `health,info` on the main port and keep metrics/prometheus on the management port. If the edge proxy is expected to block `/actuator`, say so in docs/OPERATIONS.md so the assumption is reviewable.
findings.summary: Actuator exposes health, info, metrics and prometheus, and the session filter is registered only for `/api/v1/*` (WebConfig.java:28), so those endpoints require no credential on the service port. `/actuator/metrics` and `/actuator/prometheus` disclose JVM internals, connection-pool state and per-route request volumes to anyone who can reach the port. Whether that is the internet depends on an edge configuration that is not in this repository and is not documented anywhere in docs/.

findings.suggestion: Strip or escape CR/LF (and other control characters) from any request-derived value before logging it; validating the code shape as suggested in SEC-7 also closes this, because a validated code cannot contain a newline.
findings.summary: Untrusted path input is written to the log unescaped. Tomcat percent-decodes the path before it reaches the handler, so a code containing `%0A` arrives as a real newline and is logged verbatim here and at RedirectController.java:87. An attacker can forge log lines — including plausible-looking abuse-report entries — in the log that this build relies on as the audit trail for takedowns, since no moderation console exists.

findings.suggestion: Log the link's UUID rather than its code; the UUID is already the join key for the click counters and identifies the row for any operator who needs it, without spreading the credential-like value into log aggregation.
findings.summary: Short codes are logged at INFO on create, expiry change, delete and abuse report. The design treats codes as secrets (AC16 — unguessable and non-enumerable), and this puts every issued code into the application log, where the audience is much wider than the audience for the link itself.

findings.suggestion: Add a read bucket keyed by customer id (a number in AppProperties.RateLimit, like the other four), or state explicitly in the contract that authenticated reads are unmetered by design so the omission is a decision rather than an oversight.
findings.summary: The two owner read endpoints are charged to no bucket at all — the write bucket is deliberately applied only to create/patch/delete. A single authenticated account can therefore issue unlimited `GET /api/v1/links` requests, each of which runs a paged query plus a COUNT, and each `LinkResponse` also costs a Redis round trip for the pending click delta. That is unbounded database and Redis work triggered by one caller, on the tier AC20 wants left with headroom for clicks.

findings.suggestion: Fail startup when `app.base-url` is still the localhost default outside a dev/test profile, or refuse any target whose host matches any configured serving domain rather than the single base-url host.
findings.summary: The self-referential-target check derives its host from `app.base-url`, which defaults to `http://localhost:8080`. A deployment that forgets `APP_BASE_URL` silently protects `localhost` instead of the real host, so short links pointing back at our own shortener are accepted and redirect chains loop through the service — the failure is invisible because the only symptom is a check that stops matching. It also covers exactly one host, so the planned customer-owned-domain feature will need it revisited.

not_examined: Dependency vulnerabilities: no SCA tool or advisory feed was reachable, so jjwt 0.12.6, bcprov-jdk18on 1.81, Spring Boot 3.5.16 and their transitives were not checked for known CVEs. The pinning rationale in design.json was read but not verified against advisories.

Runtime behaviour: I did not build or run the service or its test suite. All findings are from reading source, plus a small standalone JDK 21 program probing java.net.URI and InetAddress parsing to confirm SEC-2 and SEC-6.

Infrastructure outside the repository: Redis authentication, network exposure and maxmemory/eviction policy (the design flags eviction as an unresolved risk to click counts); PostgreSQL user privileges; TLS termination, HSTS and whether the edge forces HTTPS on the redirect path; whether the edge blocks /actuator (SEC-8 depends on this).

Actuator health detail behaviour under `show-details: when-authorized` with no Spring Security on the classpath was reasoned about, not verified at runtime; if it renders details unauthenticated that is a further disclosure I did not confirm.

Test sources were read only for coverage of security controls (tenant isolation, unguessability, password storage, session expiry, rate limits, denylist and internal-host rejection are all covered). I did not assess test correctness or adequacy generally — that is the test lens.

Click-path privacy: no per-click IP or user-agent is stored, but log retention, log shipping and whether remote addresses reach long-lived logs were not examined, and the requirements brief flags click-record IPs as personal data.
ClickFlushJob scheduling, the read_click_deltas.lua script and the flush/settle invariant were read for injection and error-handling only, not audited for atomicity or lost-update behaviour.
Flyway operational concerns: migration checksum drift, the stale target/classes migration that impact.json flagged, and rollback behaviour.
HTTP-level parser differentials between Tomcat, the edge proxy and browsers (request smuggling, double-decoding of the /{code} path) — this needs a live service and a fuzzing tool I do not have here.
output.summary: This is a security-literate change and most of the hard parts are right: generated codes are 128 bits of CSPRNG output with no derivation from row data; ownership is filtered inside the query rather than checked after the fetch, so "not yours" and "never existed" are one byte-identical 404; every token failure produces one indistinguishable 401; passwords are Argon2id and the unknown-account path still hashes, closing the timing oracle; every query is parameterised; the redirect scheme check rejects javascript:, data: and file: by requiring http/https on an absolute URI (confirmed against JDK parsing); nothing fetches the target server-side, so there is no classic SSRF; and the cache serialiser is typed with no polymorphic type information. The design also names its own worst hole (the alias 409 existence oracle) with reasoning attached, which is the right way to hand something to a reviewer. The weakest area is everything that depends on normalising a string into an identity. Two findings are the same mistake in different places: a host is compared to the denylist without stripping the DNS root dot (SEC-2, a working AC21 bypass), and an address literal is recognised by a dotted-quad regex that misses decimal and short forms (SEC-6). The second theme is identity of the caller: three buckets documented as "keyed by client IP" are keyed by the TCP peer, which behind the edge proxy this service is specified to sit behind means one shared bucket for everyone (SEC-3), and the limiter fails open on every bucket including sign-in (SEC-4). The one finding I would not ship past is SEC-1: fixture accounts whose passwords are published in the API specification are installed by an unconditional Flyway migration, so they exist in production, and the abuse endpoint (SEC-5) makes any account enough to take down any link on the service.

findings.suggestion: Add a class `ClickDurabilityTest` (own context, e.g. properties = "app.click.flush-interval=PT1S"): click a link N times, wait out more than one flush interval, then call resetSharedTierState() to empty the shared tier, and assert the reported count is still N. That fails against any implementation where the delta never reaches the durable column. A second method should assert the converse ordering invariant -- that no count is double-reported immediately after a flush (click N, wait a flush, read N, not 2N).
findings.summary: No test would fail if the click flush to PostgreSQL never ran. Every count assertion in the suite reads `durable + pendingDelta` (LinkService.toResponse), and the Redis hash holding the pending delta is never emptied between the clicks and the assertion. DurabilityAcrossRestartTest restarts only the application process, deliberately keeping the same Redis, so 5 clicks read back as 5 whether they reached the `links.click_count` column or are still sitting in `clicks:pending`. Delete `@Scheduled` from flush(), break read_click_deltas.lua, or break ClickFlushWriter.write and the suite stays green -- while in production the pending hash grows without bound and every counted click is lost on the first Redis eviction or restart, which is exactly the 'exact for the life of the link' claim of AC3. The harness even anticipated this test: AbstractRestartIntegrationTest.sleep is documented 'for waiting out a flush interval' and no test calls it.

findings.suggestion: Add to CustomAliasTest: `anAliasProbedBeforeItExistedRedirectsAsSoonAsItIsCreated` -- click(alias) and assert 404 (the negative entry is now cached), create a link with that alias, then click(alias) again with no evictResolutionCache() and assert 302 with the right Location. It needs its own test rather than an extra assertion in anAvailableAliasBecomesTheShortCodeExactly, because the arrangement (a prior probe) is the whole point of the behaviour.
findings.summary: `resolutionCache.invalidateBeforeIssuing(code)` on the create path is unpinned. LinkResolver caches misses for app.cache.negative-ttl (60s), so a code that was requested before it existed has a 'no such code' entry; clearing that entry at issue time is what stops a newly created link 404ing for its first minute. No test ever clicks a code and then creates a link under it: CustomAliasTest only creates-then-clicks, and RedirectTest's not-found tests never reuse the code they probed. Remove the invalidate call and nothing goes red, but a customer who checks their vanity alias before claiming it gets a link that does not work for 60 seconds -- a wiring bug the unit-level cache code cannot show.

findings.suggestion: Split out `aCreateIsRefusedWhileTheSharedTierIsUnavailable`: with Redis paused, POST /api/v1/links and assert 503, error `service_unavailable`, message 'Temporarily unable to accept new links.', and -- after resuming -- that the caller's link total did not move, so a refused create left no orphan row. Leave the click assertions where they are; they are about a different behaviour.
findings.summary: The create half of AC20 is asserted disjunctively -- `created == 201 || created == 503` -- so it cannot fail whichever way the service behaves. The design calls the 503 on create 'the only place AC20's serve-clicks-over-accepting-links preference is visible on the wire', and the implementation does refuse (ResolutionCache.invalidateBeforeIssuing throws when the shared tier is unreachable, precisely because issuing a code other instances still have cached as absent yields a dead link). Nothing in the suite requires that: an implementation that quietly issued the code anyway passes. The click side of the same test is pinned firmly, so this is one unpinned half inside an otherwise good test.

findings.suggestion: Either publish a number and assert it (e.g. in the existing hot-link test, capture per-request durations and assert a generous p95 bound such as 250ms measured in-JVM against the container, which catches an accidental per-click database round trip without being clock-flaky), or record explicitly in the artifacts that AC22's latency half is accepted as unverified so it is a decision rather than an omission.
findings.summary: AC22 has two halves -- 'continue to be served fast and counted' -- and only the counting half is pinned. aHotLinkKeepsBeingServedAndStaysExact drives 300 concurrent clicks and asserts every one was a 302 and the total is exact, but says nothing about latency; no test in the suite asserts any timing on the click path. That is partly the contract's fault: neither openapi.yaml nor design.json publishes a click-path latency number, so there is nothing to assert against, which means the 'fast' half of an acceptance criterion is shipping with no definition and no check.

findings.suggestion: Add `actuatorEndpointsStayReachableUnderTheRootRedirectMapping`: GET /actuator/health returns 200 with status UP, and GET /actuator/health is not a 302 and carries no Location. Keep it separate from the reserved-alias test -- one is about alias validation, the other about routing precedence at the root of the namespace.
findings.summary: impact.json names 'actuator endpoints staying reachable once a catch-all GET /{code} is mapped at the root' as regression surface, and no test asserts it. The nearest thing is aReservedAliasIsRejectedAsInvalidRatherThanAsAConflict, which asserts only assertNotEquals(302, api.click("actuator")) -- that passes if /actuator is 404, 500, or anything else that is not a redirect, so it demonstrates the reservation but not the thing the reservation exists to protect.

findings.suggestion: Add `ThreatCheckConfigurationTest` with two contexts: one at app.threat.enabled=false asserting Fixtures.DENYLISTED_URL is accepted with 201 (proving the check is a configurable port and that the 422 elsewhere really comes from it), and one at app.threat.fail-open=false asserting the documented refusal when the verdict is unavailable. If the second cannot be arranged without taking PostgreSQL down, say so in the artifacts rather than leaving the key unexercised.
findings.summary: The threat-check configuration surface is untested. Fixtures.THREAT_FAIL_OPEN_KEY is declared and never used by any test -- a fixture constant with no consumer is usually the fingerprint of a test that was planned and not written. Neither the fail-open branch (ThreatVerdict.UNAVAILABLE accepted with a WARN) nor the fail-closed branch (503) nor `app.threat.enabled=false` (NoOpThreatCheck) has a test, and design.json flags this reading as one of two blocking ambiguities a human never answered. AC21's positive path is well covered by CreateLinkTest, so the risk is confined to what happens when the checker cannot answer -- which is exactly the case a human is being asked to sign off blind.

findings.suggestion: Give the same @BeforeEach resetSharedTierState() to every class that asserts a specific non-2xx status on a code that does not resolve (RedirectTest, DeleteLinkTest, CustomAliasTest), or pull it up into AbstractIntegrationTest for all classes that are not counting tests. That removes an inter-class dependency whose current defence is elapsed time, which is the classic way a suite acquires a test that fails once a month and gets muted.
findings.summary: Cross-class coupling through the single JVM-wide Redis makes some 404 assertions order- and clock-dependent. Token buckets are keyed by client IP (one loopback address for the whole suite) and survive the context switch between classes; ClickRateLimitTest runs with not-found-per-minute=5 and deliberately drains that bucket. Classes that follow it and assert 404 on unissued codes -- RedirectTest (everyUnusableCodeAnswersIndistinguishably, aMalformedCodeAnswersExactlyLikeAnUnissuedOne), DeleteLinkTest, CustomAliasTest -- do not reset, so the only thing standing between them and a 429 is however much wall-clock refill happened in between. The classes that need empty buckets reset; the classes that need full ones mostly do not. AbuseReportTest and TenantIsolationTest show the authors knew the hazard and fixed it only where it had already bitten.

findings.suggestion: Either add `signInCostsTheSameWhetherOrNotTheAccountExists` with a deliberately coarse bound (e.g. median of 5 unknown-account attempts within 3x the median of 5 wrong-password attempts, tolerant enough not to flake on a loaded CI box), or record the timing half as knowingly untested. A coarse test that catches an early return is worth more than none; a tight one is worth less.
findings.summary: unknownAccountAndWrongPasswordAreRefusedIdentically pins the body half of the anti-enumeration promise but not the timing half. SignInService goes out of its way to hash against a dummy Argon2 digest when the email is unknown (absentAccountHash) precisely so the two paths cost the same; a refactor to an early return on 'no such customer' passes every test in the suite and reinstates the oracle in the one channel identical JSON cannot hide.

findings.suggestion: Keep one test named for the decision but make its assertions load-bearing -- e.g. assert the status is 302 and that the response carries the no-store headers a 301 would make pointless -- and move the 'never 301' reasoning into the javadoc where it already is, rather than into assertions that the preceding line has already guaranteed.
findings.summary: theRedirectIsTemporaryAndNeverPermanent contains two assertions that cannot fail: after assertEquals(302, status), assertNotEquals(301, status) and assertNotEquals(308, status) are implied by the first. The same shape appears at line 247 (assertNotEquals(400, ...) after assertEquals(404, ...)) and at LinkPerformanceTest:149. They read as documentation of an intent, which is useful, but a reader counting assertions overestimates what is checked, and the whole test is subsumed by aLiveShortLinkRedirectsToItsTarget.

findings.suggestion: Decide it, then pin it in its own test -- `aHeadRequestIsCountedLikeAGet` (or `...IsNotCountedAsAClick`) -- reading the count before and after a single HEAD. Do not bolt the assertion onto headAnswersLikeGetWithNoBody: that test is about response shape, and a count assertion appended to it would be masked by any earlier header failure.
findings.summary: Whether a HEAD request counts as a click is neither specified nor pinned. headAnswersLikeGetWithNoBody asserts status, Location, cache headers and an empty body, but says nothing about the counter, and the implementation counts HEAD exactly like GET because Spring dispatches it to the same handler. Under AC3 ('count every click ... as a measured number') a link checker polling HEAD hourly silently inflates a customer's reported figure. This is a contract gap as much as a test gap, but the test is where it would have surfaced.

not_examined: I did not run the suite. Testcontainers needs a Docker daemon and image pulls that this sandbox does not allow, so every claim above comes from reading sources, not from an observed pass or fail.

I did not verify the suite is currently green. triage.json records one failure (RedirectTest.aMethodOtherThanGetOrHeadIsRefusedWithoutRevealingWhetherTheCodeExists) against the pre-repair tree and a downstream coverage_floor failure caused by it; commit 6df7986 applies the adjudicated repair, but no verify has run since, so the coverage_floor outcome and the jacoco figure are unknown to me.

artifacts/test-contract.json: I mapped the 129 behaviours to classes and counted them per acceptance criterion, and read the rationale's own list of deliberate omissions, but did not re-read each behaviour statement against the method that now implements it.

artifacts/openapi.yaml (943 lines): read only through design.json's account of it. I did not walk every documented response code and header on all 8 operations and confirm an assertion exists for each; my per-endpoint checks came from the tests inward, not from the spec outward.

orchestrator/tests/test_engine.py, test_gates.py, test_graph.py: these changed substantially in the diff window (operator commits without Run-Id trailers, covering repair budget, triage routing and freeze verification). I read the added test names and one full diff, saw behaviour-specific naming and per-behaviour methods, and stopped there -- I did not read each new test body or map it to the engine.py and gates.py changes it is meant to pin.

service/src/main/resources/db/migration/V1__initial_schema.sql and the JPA entities: not reviewed for constraints (unique index on domain+code, click_count column type) that several tests implicitly depend on.

Per-source isolation of the IP-keyed CLICK, NOT_FOUND and SIGN_IN buckets (AC19's 'other customers keep being served' for those three). The test-contract states plainly why it was not attempted -- every test runs from loopback and no trusted-proxy header is in the contract -- and I agree that is the honest answer rather than a test defect, but it does mean that half of AC19 is demonstrated only on the two customer-keyed buckets.

AC17 against an actual stolen database. The schema is outside the frozen contract, so no test reads the customers table; I traced the chain instead (SignInService verifies through PasswordHasher, the seeded accounts sign in, the hasher's output is asserted to be a parameterised Argon2-shaped string) and judged it adequate, but nothing in the suite reads the stored bytes.
output.summary: This is an unusually strong suite: 129 behaviour methods across 21 classes, every one of the 22 acceptance criteria reachable from at least one test, and -- the thing that matters most for this lens -- almost every test is named for a single behaviour, arranges that behaviour itself, and asserts something specific enough to fail. I looked hard for the headline failure mode (new behaviour smuggled in as an extra assertion on an existing test) and did not find it: the assertAll blocks group assertions that genuinely belong to the same behaviour (status plus Location plus cache headers on one redirect), and where an assertion is about a different behaviour it generally has its own class (ClickRateLimitTest, SessionExpiryTest, ConfiguredDefaultExpiryTest each get their own context and property overrides rather than being folded in). The level is right too: wire behaviour is driven black-box over HTTP by a client that never follows a redirect and never throws on a status; the two things HTTP cannot see -- the code distribution and the stored credential form -- are examined at the frozen ports, and the code-generator test is a plain unit test with a bias check that no black-box test could produce. Several tests are deliberately built so they cannot pass for the wrong reason: the delete and abuse-report takedown tests refuse to clear the cache themselves and measure the elapsed time against the published 60s bound; the patch-brings-expiry-forward test relies on active invalidation because the original expiry is a month away; DurabilityAcrossRestartTest exists solely to kill the in-memory-map implementation every other test would accept. The RedirectTest 405 assertion that triage twice adjudicated as over-asserting has been repaired in 6df7986 and the replacement (compare the refusal body minus caller-known fields, plus no Location and no target leakage) is stronger than a status-only comparison, not weaker. My findings are ten, no blockers. The three that matter are behaviour with no test that would fail if it were removed: the Redis-to-PostgreSQL click flush (every count assertion is satisfied by the pending delta alone, so the entire durable-write path is invisible to the suite while the operational consequence is losing AC3's exact counts on any Redis loss); the negative-cache eviction when a code is issued (no test probes a code before creating it, so a newly created alias could 404 for 60 seconds unnoticed); and the 503-on-create under a degraded shared tier, which the degradation test tolerates disjunctively as 201-or-503 and therefore cannot fail. The rest are smaller: AC22's 'fast' half has no definition and no assertion, actuator reachability under the root catch-all was flagged in impact.json and is only weakly touched, the threat-check configuration surface is unexercised (its fixture key has no consumer), several 404 assertions depend on token buckets refilling in wall-clock time between classes, and a handful of assertions are tautological.

findings.suggestion: Normalise the host once in UrlValidator.parseOrThrow (lower-case, strip trailing dots, reject empty labels) and check and store that normalised form so denylist, own-host check and stored target all agree. Add tests asserting https://malware.example.com./x and https://MALWARE.example.com/x both return the same 422 body as the plain form. Fixing this alongside SEC-6 closes both halves of the same 'normalise a string into an identity' mistake.
findings.summary: Working AC21 bypass: URI.getHost() on https://malware.example.com./campaign returns the host with the DNS root dot, the check lower-cases but does not strip it, existsByHost misses and the parent walk yields example.com., com., '' — never the listed host. The link is created and redirects, and every resolver and browser treats the trailing dot as the same name. Verified against JDK 21 parsing by the security lens, which is why this leads the majors: it is a live control bypass with a one-character input change and a contained fix.

findings.suggestion: Reject codes that cannot exist before touching cache or database: length 1..64 and charset [A-Za-z0-9_-]. On the click path answer the standard notFound() with identical body and headers (so it stays a non-oracle) before the Redis and database round trips; on the abuse path answer the standard 202 without writing a row, so neither response becomes an existence oracle. This also closes SEC-9, since a validated code cannot contain a newline. API-2's fallback handler is still needed independently — validation removes this reachable case, not the class of cases.
findings.summary: Three lenses converged independently on the same defect: the {code} path variable is never validated for shape or length on either untrusted path. Security (SEC-7) and api-contract (API-1) both traced a code longer than 64 characters through the abuse endpoint into abuse_reports.code VARCHAR(64), raising DataIntegrityViolationException that no handler catches — the caller gets a 500 with Spring Boot's default error body where the spec (openapi.yaml:563-573) promises a uniform 202 and a closed ApiError catalogue. Performance (PERF-6) arrived at the click path from the other direction: an arbitrarily long segment becomes a Redis GET key, a PostgreSQL parameter and a negatively-cached entry whose size an attacker chooses, on the one endpoint that is unauthenticated. Convergence from three framings on one unvalidated input raises confidence to high; the severity is api-contract's major, since an untrusted input turning into an unhandled 500 is the concrete part.

findings.suggestion: Add a fallback @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) that logs and returns a fixed ApiError body, then either document a 500 entry in the error catalogue or map the reachable dependency failures onto documented statuses (API-3). Clear, small fix; do it even after SEC-7's validation lands, because validation removes one reachable case and not the class.
findings.summary: ApiExceptionHandler covers five exception types and nothing else, so any other RuntimeException on the management surface (Postgres outage mid-request, Jackson serialization failure, the DataIntegrityViolation of SEC-7) falls through to Boot's BasicErrorController and answers 500 with {timestamp,status,error,path} rather than ApiError. openapi.yaml:47 declares the catalogue closed and every non-2xx body ApiError-shaped; 500 appears nowhere in the document. The click path made this decision deliberately (RedirectController:86, see API-8); the management path is the framework default leaking through at the one point nobody decided.

findings.suggestion: Fetch all pending deltas for the page in one opsForHash().multiGet(pendingKey, codes) — HMGET is single-key so it keeps the Cluster-safety property the class documents — and do it after the transaction returns rather than inside it.
findings.summary: GET /api/v1/links maps every row through toResponse, which calls clickCounter.pendingDelta per link — one sequential Redis HGET per item, up to 100 (MAX_PAGE_SIZE), inside a readOnly @Transactional that has already acquired a Hikari connection. With the configured 1s Redis timeout, a degraded-but-alive Redis makes one list request hold a database connection for up to 100 seconds; ten such requests exhaust the default pool of 10 and stall every other endpoint, including a redirect that missed cache. SEC-11 notes the same endpoint is charged to no rate-limit bucket, so a single account can drive this at will — the two compound and are worth fixing together.

findings.suggestion: Replace HGETALL with HSCAN in a loop inside the script until `limit` fields are collected, persisting the cursor (or using a per-pass random start) so passes make progress across the hash; keep the zero-field sweep on the scanned window. Confirm with redis-cli --latency or SLOWLOG during a pass against a synthetically large pending hash.
findings.summary: readPending bounds what it returns (limit) but not what it reads: the script HGETALLs the entire pending hash and discards everything past the limit, so the batch is O(total pending links) in Redis CPU and Lua memory every 5 seconds on every instance. Redis is single-threaded for scripts, so once the hash has grown (PERF-1) the background job stalls the same Redis that serves the resolution cache and the rate limiter on the redirect hot path; the 1s command timeout then converts that into cache misses and fail-open rate limiting rather than an outage. Put first among the click-drain findings because it has a bounded, mechanical fix.

findings.suggestion: Add ClickDurabilityTest in its own context (app.click.flush-interval=PT1S): click a link N times, wait out more than one flush interval, call resetSharedTierState() to empty the shared tier, and assert the reported count is still N. Add the converse ordering assertion (click N, wait a flush, read N and not 2N). The harness already anticipated this — AbstractRestartIntegrationTest.sleep is documented 'for waiting out a flush interval' and no test calls it.
findings.summary: No test would fail if the click flush to PostgreSQL never ran: every count assertion reads durable + pendingDelta and the Redis hash is never emptied between the clicks and the assertion, and DurabilityAcrossRestartTest deliberately keeps the same Redis across the restart. Delete @Scheduled from flush(), break read_click_deltas.lua or break ClickFlushWriter.write and the suite stays green. Read together with PERF-1 and PERF-2 this is the most important cluster in the review: the subsystem carrying AC3's 'exact for the life of the link' claim has a throughput ceiling nobody measured, a scan cost nobody bounded, and no test that would notice if the durable write path were removed entirely.

findings.suggestion: Split out aCreateIsRefusedWhileTheSharedTierIsUnavailable: with Redis paused, POST /api/v1/links and assert 503, error service_unavailable, message 'Temporarily unable to accept new links.', and after resuming that the caller's link total did not move so a refused create left no orphan row. Leave the click assertions where they are.
findings.summary: The create half of AC20 is asserted disjunctively (created == 201 || created == 503), so it cannot fail whichever way the service behaves. The design calls the 503-on-create 'the only place AC20's serve-clicks-over-accepting-links preference is visible on the wire' and the implementation does refuse, but an implementation that quietly issued the code anyway passes. The click side of the same test is pinned firmly, so this is one unpinned half inside an otherwise good test — and it is the half API-3 shows is already narrower than the spec claims.

findings.suggestion: Add to CustomAliasTest: anAliasProbedBeforeItExistedRedirectsAsSoonAsItIsCreated — click(alias) and assert 404, create a link with that alias, click(alias) again with no evictResolutionCache() and assert 302 with the right Location. Give it its own test rather than an extra assertion, because the prior probe is the whole arrangement.
findings.summary: resolutionCache.invalidateBeforeIssuing(code) on the create path is unpinned: LinkResolver caches misses for 60s, so a code probed before it existed carries a 'no such code' entry, and clearing that at issue time is what stops a newly created link 404ing for its first minute. No test ever clicks a code and then creates a link under it — CustomAliasTest only creates-then-clicks and RedirectTest never reuses a probed code. Remove the invalidate call and nothing goes red, while a customer who checks their vanity alias before claiming it gets a link that does not work for a minute.

findings.suggestion: Make the failure mode per bucket: keep fail-open for CLICK (that rationale is sound and AC20 asks for it) and fail closed — or fall back to a small in-process per-instance bucket — for SIGN_IN, WRITE and ABUSE_REPORT, where refusing is the safe direction. Independently, bound password verification with a semaphore or small dedicated executor sized to available cores, returning 503/429 when saturated, so credential-stuffing load cannot displace redirects regardless of the limiter's state. Add a test asserting sign-in is still throttled with the Redis container stopped, and measure p99 redirect latency while replaying concurrent sign-in failures.
findings.summary: Security and performance converged on the same defect from opposite ends: nothing bounds unauthenticated memory-hard work. The limiter fails open for every bucket, not just the click path the rationale justifies, so a Redis outage removes brute-force and credential-stuffing protection at the moment the service is already unhappy (SEC-4); and even with the limiter healthy, nothing caps concurrent Argon2id — Tomcat's default 200 request threads means up to 200 simultaneous hashes at m=16384 KiB, roughly 3.2 GiB of transient allocation and full CPU saturation, sharing the heap and thread pool with the redirect path (PERF-8). The click path is itself the cheapest way to pressure the shared Redis that is the only brake. Two independent lenses reaching this raises confidence; it needs two distinct fixes, not one.

findings.suggestion: Map DataAccessResourceFailureException/CannotCreateTransactionException on the create path onto ApiException.dependencyUnavailable so the documented 503 is what a caller sees; alternatively document that 503 covers only the cache and threat tiers, which is a weaker promise than openapi.yaml:325 currently makes. Whichever is chosen, TEST-3's split-out test should assert it.
findings.summary: openapi.yaml:324-337 documents 503 on POST /api/v1/links for 'a dependency the create path needs is unavailable', but 503 is produced in exactly three places — code exhaustion, the threat checker with fail-open disabled (fail-open is true by default), and the resolution cache. PostgreSQL, the dependency most likely to be unavailable, is not one of them: saveAndFlush throws a DataAccessException that reaches no handler and answers 500 with the framework body. The documented degradation story for AC20 therefore does not hold for the most probable outage. Ranked below API-2 because it needs a decision about which promise moves, not just a handler.

findings.suggestion: Either set server.forward-headers-strategy: native|framework and have the edge overwrite (not append to) X-Forwarded-For, or state in the contract that the edge owns per-IP limiting and drop the app-side IP buckets. Do not read X-Forwarded-For without a trusted-proxy list — that hands the limit key to the attacker. A test driving two requests with different forwarded addresses through one socket would pin whichever choice is made.
findings.summary: The three buckets the contract documents as 'keyed by client IP' (click, not-found, sign-in) are keyed by request.getRemoteAddr(), and nothing sets server.forward-headers-strategy. Behind any load balancer that is the proxy's address for every request: per-source throttling for AC19 does not distinguish sources at all, and the global caps become a self-inflicted denial of service — 3000 clicks/min and 60 sign-ins/min for the entire service against a target of ~100M clicks/day. Same call at SignInController:40. This is a deployment-shape decision as much as a code fix, which is why it sits below the mechanical majors; the test lens independently noted (TEST-7, and in its not_examined) that per-source isolation of these buckets is untestable from loopback, so nothing in the suite would reveal it either.

findings.suggestion: Add a per-reporter daily cap distinct from the per-minute bucket, and require a second distinct reporter or operator confirmation before blocking a link above a click threshold. Independently add an operator-only unblock path so an incorrect takedown is recoverable; the audit rows already record who reported what. This reverses a clarification a human already signed off, so it wants that human rather than a unilateral change.
findings.summary: Any signed-in customer can permanently disable any link whose code they have seen, and codes are seen by everyone handed the link. The takedown is immediate and irreversible in this build — updateExpiry answers 409 for a non-ACTIVE link and there is no unblock path — so a false or malicious takedown needs a DBA. Clarification Q4 accepted the mechanism on 'rate-limited per reporter' plus an audit row, but the limit is 60/min (86,400 links a day from one account), which does not bound the attack the design said it bounded, and the accepted reasoning did not consider irreversibility. SEC-1 makes this worse: the seeded accounts are enough. Note SEC-9 also undermines the audit row this design leans on, and API-6 shows the block can be overwritten by a subsequent owner delete.

findings.suggestion: Batch the durable writes — one transaction per pass with a multi-row update or a JDBC batch of `update links set click_count = click_count + ? where id = ?` — and pipeline the settle decrements, then raise flush-batch-size and measure drain rate against arrival rate. Before shipping, expose HLEN clicks:pending as a gauge and alert on an upward trend; a monotonically growing pending hash is the signal that the drain is behind and it is currently invisible.
findings.summary: The click drain has a hard ceiling of 500 distinct links per 5s pass, each costing one JPA transaction plus one Redis settle round trip, sequentially on one scheduler thread — about 100 distinct links/second per instance against a design that reasons about 100M links/day. Every replica runs the same unsharded schedule, so replicas multiply reads of the same hash rather than dividing work; above that arrival rate the pending hash only grows, which is what feeds PERF-2. Placed last among the majors because unlike the others it is structural: the fix is a redesign of the drain, not an edit, and TEST-1 means nothing in the suite would show it either way.

findings.suggestion: Treat any host containing no alphabetic character as an address literal and run it through InetAddress.getByName before isInternalAddress, which covers decimal, octal and short-form IPv4 in one line. The DNS-name case is documented as deliberately out of scope and can stay that way.
findings.summary: The loopback/private/link-local check is bypassable with non-dotted-quad address literals: IPV4_LITERAL matches only d.d.d.d, so http://2130706433/ and http://0/ are treated as ordinary names and InetAddress is never consulted (verified on JDK 21). Impact is bounded because nothing fetches the target server-side, so this is not SSRF — it is the shortener being usable to point clickers at loopback and LAN addresses under our name, which is the case the 422 rule exists to prevent. Same root cause as SEC-2; fix them in one sitting.

findings.suggestion: Strip or escape CR/LF and other control characters from any request-derived value before logging. Validating the code shape per SEC-7 also closes this, so sequence SEC-7 first and this becomes a defence-in-depth change.
findings.summary: Untrusted path input is logged unescaped. Tomcat percent-decodes the path before the handler, so a code containing %0A arrives as a real newline and is logged verbatim here and at RedirectController:87, letting an attacker forge log lines — including plausible abuse-report entries — in the log this build relies on as the takedown audit trail, since no moderation console exists. That makes it a direct amplifier of SEC-5 rather than a standalone logging nit.

findings.suggestion: Make the configured value load-bearing or delete it. Cheapest consistent option: have LinkPolicyConfig.urlValidator(...) pass properties.links().maxUrlLength() into UrlValidator (it already passes baseUrl) and drop the hardcoded constant; keep @Size(max = 2048) only by referencing a shared compile-time constant.
findings.summary: The maximum long-URL length exists three times and two agree only by accident: UrlValidator.MAX_URL_LENGTH = 2048, @Size(max = 2048) on CreateLinkRequest.longUrl, and app.links.max-url-length: 2048 bound to AppProperties.Links.maxUrlLength, which no code reads. Raising the limit in config changes nothing and a reviewer would reasonably believe it did — the dangerous kind of duplication, because the dead copy is the one that looks authoritative.

findings.suggestion: Write @Pattern(regexp = AliasPolicy.PATTERN) — it is a public static final String and so a valid annotation constant — and delete the comment. If the package cycle is unwanted, move PATTERN to the api package and have AliasPolicy reference it.
findings.summary: The alias charset rule is a literal regex on the DTO and again as AliasPolicy.PATTERN, which carries the comment 'identical to the one on the request DTO' — documenting the drift risk rather than removing it. PATTERN also duplicates MIN_LENGTH/MAX_LENGTH inside its own literal. Worth fixing in the same pass as SEC-7, which adds a third place that needs the same charset.

findings.suggestion: Drop the inline default — @Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "${app.click.flush-interval}") — since @DefaultValue("PT5S") plus application.yml already supply it, and comment AppProperties.Click.flushInterval to say it is consumed by the annotation, so the accessor does not read as dead.
findings.summary: @Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "${app.click.flush-interval:PT5S}") reaches past the typed AppProperties surface the rest of the change uses uniformly and restates the PT5S default AppProperties.Click.flushInterval already declares, so that accessor is read by nothing and the documented value can diverge silently from the actual schedule. Same file as PERF-1 and TEST-1: whoever touches the flush job should land all three.

findings.suggestion: Delete the unused LinkEntity.isResolvableAt and let CachedLink.redirectsAt be the single statement of the rule, or express both in terms of one static predicate on LinkStatus. Either way one of the two should stop existing.
findings.summary: 'A link redirects when it is ACTIVE and not yet expired' is expressed twice — CachedLink.redirectsAt and LinkEntity.statusAt/isResolvableAt — and they must agree: a fourth LinkStatus, or moving the expiry boundary from exclusive to inclusive, has to be done in both. LinkEntity.isResolvableAt is currently called by nothing, so nothing would fail if only one copy were updated.

findings.suggestion: Bind actuator to a separate management port on the internal interface (management.server.port), or expose only health,info on the main port and keep metrics/prometheus on the management port. Either way document the decision — in the spec or a note stating the surface is operational and outside the public contract — and if the edge is expected to block /actuator, say so in docs/OPERATIONS.md so the assumption is reviewable. TEST-5 is the matching test gap.
findings.summary: Security and api-contract converged on the actuator surface from different angles, which is why confidence here is high: health, info, metrics and prometheus are exposed on the service port and the session filter is registered only for /api/v1/* (WebConfig:28), so they need no credential (SEC-8), and they appear nowhere in openapi.yaml, whose 'Two surfaces' table lists only the management API and the click path (API-5). /actuator/metrics and /actuator/prometheus disclose JVM internals, pool state and per-route request volumes; whether that reaches the internet depends on edge configuration that is neither in this repository nor documented in docs/. Undocumented surface becomes a de facto contract the moment a probe depends on it.

findings.suggestion: Drop @Transactional from resolve(), let the repository call use its own transaction, and perform cache.put after it returns. Confirm with a Hikari connections-usage histogram comparing hit and miss requests.
findings.summary: resolve() is @Transactional(readOnly = true) and the cache.put happens inside it, after the JDBC statement has acquired a connection. Hibernate's delayed acquisition means a cache hit costs no connection, but every miss holds a pooled connection across a Redis PUT with a 1s timeout — connection-hold time proportional to Redis latency on the one path that must not queue. The transaction buys nothing: it wraps a single read.

findings.suggestion: Add actuatorEndpointsStayReachableUnderTheRootRedirectMapping: GET /actuator/health returns 200 with status UP, is not a 302 and carries no Location. Keep it separate from the reserved-alias test — one is about alias validation, the other about routing precedence at the root of the namespace.
findings.summary: impact.json names 'actuator endpoints staying reachable once a catch-all GET /{code} is mapped at the root' as regression surface and no test asserts it. The nearest thing asserts only assertNotEquals(302, api.click("actuator")), which passes if /actuator is 404 or 500 — it demonstrates the reservation but not the thing the reservation exists to protect. Pairs with SEC-8: the same surface is untested and undocumented.

findings.suggestion: Give the same @BeforeEach resetSharedTierState() to every class that asserts a specific non-2xx status on a code that does not resolve, or pull it into AbstractIntegrationTest for all classes that are not counting tests.
findings.summary: Cross-class coupling through the JVM-wide Redis makes some 404 assertions order- and clock-dependent: token buckets are keyed by client IP (one loopback address for the whole suite) and survive the context switch, and ClickRateLimitTest runs with not-found-per-minute=5 and deliberately drains that bucket. RedirectTest, DeleteLinkTest and CustomAliasTest then assert 404 on unissued codes with nothing between them and a 429 but wall-clock refill. AbuseReportTest and TenantIsolationTest reset, showing the authors knew the hazard and fixed it only where it had already bitten — this is how a suite acquires a test that fails once a month and gets muted.

findings.suggestion: Add ThreatCheckConfigurationTest with two contexts: app.threat.enabled=false asserting Fixtures.DENYLISTED_URL is accepted with 201 (proving the check is a configurable port and the 422 elsewhere really comes from it), and app.threat.fail-open=false asserting the documented refusal when the verdict is unavailable. If the second cannot be arranged without taking PostgreSQL down, record that in the artifacts rather than leaving the key unexercised.
findings.summary: The threat-check configuration surface is entirely unexercised: Fixtures.THREAT_FAIL_OPEN_KEY is declared and used by no test — the fingerprint of a test planned and not written — and neither the fail-open branch (UNAVAILABLE accepted with a WARN), nor the fail-closed 503, nor app.threat.enabled=false has a test. design.json flags this reading as one of two blocking ambiguities a human never answered, so the unverified branch is precisely the one someone is being asked to sign off blind. AC21's positive path is well covered, so the risk is confined to what happens when the checker cannot answer.

findings.suggestion: Add a read bucket keyed by customer id (a number in AppProperties.RateLimit like the other four), or state in the contract that authenticated reads are unmetered by design so the omission is a decision rather than an oversight.
findings.summary: The two owner read endpoints are charged to no bucket at all — the write bucket is applied only to create/patch/delete — so one authenticated account can issue unlimited GET /api/v1/links, each running a paged query plus a COUNT (PERF-7) and one Redis round trip per row (PERF-3). Unbounded database and Redis work from a single caller, on the tier AC20 wants left with headroom for clicks. Two lenses reached this endpoint by different routes; the rate-limit gap is what turns their cost findings into an availability one.

findings.suggestion: Decide and record which side moves: either set spring.mvc.throw-exception-if-no-handler-found and handle NoResourceFoundException/HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException into ApiError, or state in the spec that dispatcher-level 404/405 responses carry the container's body and are outside the closed catalogue.
findings.summary: Dispatcher-level refusals on the management surface return the framework error body rather than ApiError: an unknown path under /api/v1 with a valid token (NoResourceFoundException -> 404) and a wrong method on a documented path (PUT /api/v1/links/{code} -> 405). openapi.yaml:29-43 promises the not-found body byte for byte 'on both surfaces' and :47 promises ApiError for every non-2xx; Note 2 exempts only the /{code} 405 status, not the body shape, and says nothing about the management surface. Same closed-catalogue promise as API-2, one layer further out.

findings.suggestion: Decide which side is right and write it down. If BLOCKED must survive a delete, make markDeleted conditional the way markBlocked is and keep answering 204 (idempotent, no new status). If an owner may relabel their blocked link, say so in the DELETE description, because a reader of the PATCH 409 rationale will assume the opposite.
findings.summary: DELETE on the caller's own BLOCKED link answers 204 and overwrites the status to DELETED (markDeleted is unconditional, unlike markBlocked at LinkEntity:139, which deliberately refuses to overwrite). That conforms on status — DELETE documents no 409 — but the representation diverges: GET afterwards reports DELETED for a link taken down for abuse, so the takedown becomes invisible in the API. Read alongside SEC-5, which notes there is no unblock path and no moderation console: this is the one way a block silently stops being visible, and the abuse audit trail is the only remaining record.

findings.suggestion: Pipeline the rate-limit and cache GET into one round trip (both are needed unconditionally), and/or issue the HINCRBY asynchronously on the Lettuce connection without awaiting the reply — this differs from the executor-with-a-queue the javadoc rightly rejects, since it drops nothing. At minimum lower the command timeout for the increment specifically, and measure redirect p99 against a latency-injected Redis.
findings.summary: A served redirect makes three sequential Redis round trips (rate-limit script, cache GET, click HINCRBY) before the 302 is written, four on a not-found, each carrying the 1s command timeout — so a Redis that is slow rather than down can add ~3s to a redirect otherwise servable from cached data, and the increment delays the response purely to record a statistic. This is a documented deliberate trade (ClickCounter javadoc, AC3) rather than an oversight; kept at minor and stated plainly because it is the tail PERF-2's stalls would land on, and TEST-4 shows nothing measures redirect latency at all.

findings.suggestion: Set spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size explicitly with a comment tying it to expected concurrency and PostgreSQL max_connections, and consider per-code single-flight (a striped lock or loading wrapper on the miss path) so a hot link's TTL expiry produces one database read rather than one per in-flight click. Measure hikaricp.connections.pending and the redirect miss ratio under sustained load.
findings.summary: No pool sizing is configured, so Hikari runs at its default maximum of 10 connections and nothing configures the Lettuce or Tomcat side either. That meets a structural property: app.cache.ttl is pinned at 60s to floor the takedown bound, so every actively-clicked link is re-read from PostgreSQL at least once per minute per replica, and with no single-flight, N concurrent clicks on a link whose entry just expired all miss and all issue the same lookup. The database read rate has a floor of (distinct active links)/60s served through 10 connections — the pool, not the indexed query, is the ceiling, and nobody picked the number deliberately. PERF-3 and PERF-4 are what consume that pool from elsewhere.

findings.suggestion: If the totals must stay in the contract, at least bound page (or cap offset) the way size is capped in requireValidPaging. Longer term, keyset pagination on (created_at desc, code asc) removes both the count and the offset walk. Confirm with EXPLAIN ANALYZE of the count query against a customer with ~1M links.
findings.summary: findOwnedBy returns Page, so every list request issues a count query, and LinkPage exposes totalElements/totalPages so it cannot be dropped without an API change. The count scans the whole customer_id range of ix_links_owner_listing on each page request, and offset paging compounds it — page is unbounded, so page=100000 makes PostgreSQL walk and discard the offset rows. This is the management endpoint rather than the hot path, so the blast radius is one caller's latency and the connection they hold — except that SEC-11 leaves that caller unmetered.

findings.suggestion: Either publish a number and assert it (capture per-request durations in the existing hot-link test and assert a generous p95 bound such as 250ms in-JVM against the container, which catches an accidental per-click database round trip without being clock-flaky), or record in the artifacts that AC22's latency half is knowingly unverified so it is a decision rather than an omission.
findings.summary: AC22 has two halves — 'continue to be served fast and counted' — and only counting is pinned: aHotLinkKeepsBeingServedAndStaysExact drives 300 concurrent clicks and asserts every one was a 302 and the total exact, but no test in the suite asserts any timing on the click path. That is partly the contract's fault, since neither openapi.yaml nor design.json publishes a latency number, so the 'fast' half of an acceptance criterion is shipping with no definition and no check — and PERF-9 and PERF-2 are precisely the mechanisms that would move it.

findings.suggestion: Move the container-independent helpers to static methods on ApiClient or Fixtures (Fixtures.givenLink(api, bearer), ApiClient.clickRepeatedly(api, code, times)) and have both base classes delegate, so the restart harness inherits nothing but still shares one definition of each helper. Worth doing before TEST-1's durability test lands, since that test needs the restart harness's sleep helper.
findings.summary: alice(), bob(), givenLink(bearer), sleep(Duration) and clickRepeatedly(...) are re-implemented alongside AbstractIntegrationTest. The class comment explains convincingly why the two cannot share a superclass, but that argument does not extend to the helpers — and clickRepeatedly has already drifted: it returns List<Integer> here and List<HttpResponse<String>> there, so the same name means two things depending on which base class a test extends.

findings.suggestion: Update §7 to match the delivered contract (or mark it superseded by artifacts/design.json), and point the CacheConfig javadoc at something that exists — the negative-caching rationale is already written in LinkResolver and CachedLink.
findings.summary: §7 of the committed 'plan of record' now contradicts the service that was built: 410-for-expired vs 404-for-unknown (the design deliberately chose 404 for both), 'Caffeine only — no Redis in the build' (the change is Redis-backed throughout), a /api/v1/links/{code}/stats endpoint, Idempotency-Key, an outbox, and 7-character codes (shipped: 22). Relatedly CacheConfig.LINKS_CACHE cites 'the enumeration note in ADR-004', but no ADR documents exist in the repo and the only ADR-004 reference is this plan's superseded code-length decision. Documentation that confidently describes a different system is worse than none.

findings.suggestion: Replace \' with ' in the three AbuseReportService javadoc lines and add the java.util.UUID import in SignInService.
findings.summary: Javadoc contains escaped apostrophes (competitor\'s, customer\'s on lines 35-36) — a shell-escaping artifact that renders literally in generated docs — and SignInService.java:46 writes java.util.UUID.randomUUID() fully qualified where every other file imports UUID. Trivial and mechanical; listed first among the nits because it can be fixed without thinking.

findings.suggestion: Add spring.jackson.serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps: false explicitly, next to the deserialization block already pinned for the same reason.
findings.summary: The spec freezes the timestamp format (openapi.yaml:67, ISO-8601 instants in UTC) and the config pins fail-on-unknown-properties for the strict-body rule right beside it, but nothing pins serialization.write-dates-as-timestamps. The contract-correct rendering of createdAt/expiresAt therefore rests on a Spring Boot default. The default is currently right, so this is not a live divergence — only an unpinned one on a value the spec calls frozen.

findings.suggestion: Either store and query email lower-cased (as threat_denylist.host already does, with a comment explaining exactly this reasoning), or add CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_customers_email_lower ON customers (lower(email)) and query with a matching predicate. Confirm with EXPLAIN on the generated statement.
findings.summary: findByEmailIgnoreCase generates upper(email) = upper(?), which cannot use the ux_customers_email btree index, so every sign-in is a sequential scan of customers. Today that is two seeded rows and there is no registration endpoint, so the cost is nil; it is filed because the index exists and reads as if it serves this lookup, and the day accounts arrive the scan arrives with them. Note SEC-1's fix removes those two rows from production, which changes who this affects but not the shape.

findings.suggestion: Fail startup when app.base-url is still the localhost default outside a dev/test profile, or refuse any target whose host matches any configured serving domain rather than the single base-url host.
findings.summary: The self-referential-target check derives its host from app.base-url, which defaults to http://localhost:8080, so a deployment that forgets APP_BASE_URL silently protects localhost instead of the real host and short links pointing back at our own shortener are accepted, looping redirect chains through the service. The failure is invisible because the only symptom is a check that stops matching. It also covers exactly one host, so the planned customer-owned-domain feature will need it revisited. Same class of silent-default risk as SEC-1's unconditional migration.

findings.suggestion: Log the link's UUID rather than its code; the UUID is already the join key for the click counters and identifies the row for any operator who needs it, without spreading a credential-like value into log aggregation. Note this trades against SEC-9's audit-trail concern — the abuse log line still needs to identify the link, so use the UUID there too rather than dropping the field.
findings.summary: Short codes are logged at INFO on create, expiry change, delete and abuse report. The design treats codes as secrets (AC16 — unguessable and non-enumerable), and this puts every issued code into the application log, whose audience is much wider than the audience for the link itself.

findings.suggestion: Keep one test named for the decision but make its assertions load-bearing — assert 302 and that the response carries the no-store headers a 301 would make pointless — and move the 'never 301' reasoning into the javadoc where it already is.
findings.summary: theRedirectIsTemporaryAndNeverPermanent contains two assertions that cannot fail: after assertEquals(302, status), assertNotEquals(301, ...) and assertNotEquals(308, ...) are implied. The same shape appears at line 247 and at LinkPerformanceTest:149. They read as documentation of intent, which is useful, but a reader counting assertions overestimates what is checked — and this suite's assertion count is otherwise a reliable signal, which is why it is worth tidying.

findings.suggestion: Decide it, then pin it in its own test — aHeadRequestIsCountedLikeAGet or ...IsNotCountedAsAClick — reading the count before and after a single HEAD. Do not bolt the assertion onto headAnswersLikeGetWithNoBody: that test is about response shape and a count assertion there would be masked by any earlier header failure.
findings.summary: Whether a HEAD request counts as a click is neither specified nor pinned: headAnswersLikeGetWithNoBody asserts status, Location, cache headers and empty body but says nothing about the counter, and the implementation counts HEAD exactly like GET because Spring dispatches it to the same handler. Under AC3 a link checker polling HEAD hourly silently inflates a customer's reported figure. This is a contract gap as much as a test gap — the api-contract lens separately recorded that HEAD dispatch was assumed framework behaviour and not verified.

findings.suggestion: Either add signInCostsTheSameWhetherOrNotTheAccountExists with a deliberately coarse bound (median of 5 unknown-account attempts within 3x the median of 5 wrong-password attempts, tolerant enough not to flake on a loaded CI box), or record the timing half as knowingly untested. A coarse test that catches an early return is worth more than none; a tight one is worth less.
findings.summary: unknownAccountAndWrongPasswordAreRefusedIdentically pins the body half of the anti-enumeration promise but not the timing half. SignInService deliberately hashes against a dummy Argon2 digest when the email is unknown precisely so the two paths cost the same; a refactor to an early return on 'no such customer' passes every test in the suite and reinstates the oracle in the one channel identical JSON cannot hide. Note that SEC-4/PERF-8's suggested concurrency bound on hashing must preserve this property.

findings.suggestion: Either drop the ones with no caller, or add a single line to each saying it is contract surface retained for future callers, so a later reader does not have to grep the repo to find out.
findings.summary: A handful of members exist for tests that never call them: UrlValidator.ownHost() and its no-arg constructor, ShortCodeGenerator.random() and its SecureRandom constructor, RateLimitDecision.remaining(), LinkEntity.getDomain()/getCustomerId(). They were plausibly frozen into the contract before the tests were written, which is a real reason, but as shipped they are surface nobody exercises. CLEAN-4's LinkEntity.isResolvableAt belongs to the same set.

findings.suggestion: No code change implied by the contract. Consider a sentence in the /{code} 404 description recording that an internal failure is also answered this way, so the 404 is not read as a positive assertion that the code was never issued. An alert on the catch-block log line is the operational half of this.
findings.summary: The click path catches every RuntimeException and answers the documented 404, which honours 'this operation never returns 5xx' (openapi.yaml:601) with a byte-exact body and cache headers — but it means a PostgreSQL outage renders every live link as 'does not resolve', indistinguishable to a caller from mass deletion. The contract offers no other status, so the code is following it; the lens filed this as a consequence for a reviewer's eye rather than a defect, and I agree — it is last because no change is implied, not because it is unimportant. It is also the counterpart to API-2: the click path decided this deliberately and the management path did not.

output.summary: Strong, security-literate change: contract conformance is near-exact on all eight operations, the single-404 rule and tenant isolation hold, the redirect hot path is a well-built cache-plus-index lookup, and the test suite is unusually good (129 behaviour methods, almost all named for one behaviour and asserting something that can fail). Look first at SEC-1, the only blocker and the only finding that should pause shipping: two customer accounts whose plaintext passwords are published in openapi.yaml are installed in every environment by an unconditional Flyway migration, and since there is no registration endpoint they are the accounts — which SEC-5 (any account can irreversibly take down any link) turns from an embarrassment into a live takeover path. After that, three clusters cost real time: string normalisation as identity (SEC-2's trailing-dot denylist bypass is a working AC21 defeat with a contained fix, SEC-6 the same mistake on address literals), unvalidated input reaching the framework floor (SEC-7/API-1/PERF-6 converged on the unvalidated {code}, and API-2 shows there is no fallback exception handler behind it), and the click-counting subsystem, where PERF-1's ~100 links/sec drain ceiling, PERF-2's unbounded HGETALL and TEST-1's finding that no test would fail if the durable write were deleted all describe one under-verified path carrying AC3's exactness claim. Everything else is minors and nits, several of which are one-line fixes worth batching.
top_risks: Nothing in this review was executed. All five lenses read source only: no build, no test run, no query plan, no wire capture (security ran a small standalone JDK probe for SEC-2/SEC-6, and that is the extent of observed behaviour anywhere). The test lens further notes the suite's greenness is unknown to it — triage.json records a failure against the pre-repair tree and a downstream coverage_floor failure, commit 6df7986 applies the adjudicated repair, and no verify has run since. A green verify is a precondition for reading any of this as a review of working software.

The click-counting subsystem is unverified from every direction at once and stays risky even after each individual finding is fixed. No lens read redis/token_bucket.lua or audited read_click_deltas.lua for atomicity (performance read it for cost, security for injection only, cleanliness for existence); no lens reasoned through the flush/settle invariant under more than one replica (performance took RedisClickCounter's javadoc on trust); and Redis maxmemory and eviction policy are outside the repository and were examined by nobody, which is what actually decides whether a growing pending hash loses counts or stalls the hot path. AC3's 'exact for the life of the link' currently rests on an unread script, an unexercised durable write and an unknown eviction policy.

The service's behaviour behind its edge proxy is assumed, not specified. SEC-3 shows the three IP-keyed buckets are keyed by the TCP peer with no forwarded-headers strategy; SEC-8/API-5 shows /actuator/metrics and /actuator/prometheus are unauthenticated and whether they reach the internet depends on edge config not in this repository and not in docs/; the security lens also did not examine TLS termination, HSTS or HTTP parser differentials between Tomcat and the edge. Fixing the findings does not produce a reviewable statement of what the edge is responsible for — and the test lens confirms per-source rate-limit isolation (half of AC19) cannot be demonstrated at all while every test runs from loopback.

No supply-chain check was performed by anyone. Security could not reach an SCA tool or advisory feed, so jjwt 0.12.6, bcprov-jdk18on 1.81, Spring Boot 3.5.16 and their transitives are unchecked for known CVEs; cleanliness explicitly deferred pom.xml dependency and version choices to that lens. A dependency scan should run before release regardless of the findings above.

Two acceptance criteria are shipping without a definition rather than without a test. AC22's 'fast' half has no published latency number in openapi.yaml or design.json, so TEST-4 has nothing to assert against and PERF-9's three sequential Redis round trips per redirect have no budget to violate; and design.json's threat-check fail-open reading is recorded as a blocking ambiguity a human never answered, with TEST-6 confirming no test exercises either branch. Both need a decision from a person, not a code change.

Operational visibility is thin exactly where the structural risks are. PERF-1 notes HLEN clicks:pending — the one signal that would show the drain falling behind — is not exposed; no alert exists on RedirectController's catch-all, so API-8's 'a database outage renders every link as not-found' would be silent; and SEC-5's takedown audit trail is a log the SEC-9 log-injection defect lets an attacker forge. Even a fully fixed version of this change would be hard to diagnose in production.
